title: Exodus

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 1
summaryBullets: These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob, each with his family: (1:1).
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah; (1:2).
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin; (1:3).
Dan and Naphtali; Gad and Asher. (1:4).
The descendants of Jacob numbered seventy in all, including Joseph, who was already in Egypt. (1:5).
Now Joseph and all his brothers and all that generation died, (1:6).
but the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous, so that the land was filled with them. (1:7).
Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power in Egypt. (1:8).
“Look,” he said to his people, “the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us. (1:9).
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more; and if a war breaks out, they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.” (1:10).
So the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. As a result, they built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh. (1:11).
But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished; so the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites. (1:12).
They worked the Israelites ruthlessly (1:13).
and made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields. Every service they imposed was harsh. (1:14).
Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, whose names were Shiphrah and Puah, (1:15).
“When you help the Hebrew women give birth, observe them on the birthstools. If the child is a son, kill him; but if it is a daughter, let her live.” (1:16).
The midwives, however, feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live. (1:17).
So the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and asked them, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?” (1:18).
The midwives answered Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before a midwife arrives.” (1:19).
So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous. (1:20).
And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own. (1:21).
Then Pharaoh commanded all his people: “Every son born to the Hebrews you must throw into the Nile, but every daughter you may allow to live.” (1:22).
crossRefs: Genesis 46:26-27: Seventy persons of Jacob's house go down into Egypt, the number this chapter opens with.
Genesis 15:13-14: God tells Abraham his offspring will be enslaved and afflicted in a foreign land, then come out with great possessions.
Genesis 47:11: Joseph settles his father and brothers in the district of Rameses, the best of the land of Egypt.
Acts 7:17-19: Stephen recounts the king who dealt shrewdly with Israel and forced them to expose their infants.
Matthew 2:16: Herod orders the killing of every boy in Bethlehem two years old and under.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פַּרְעֹה (paroh), from Egyptian pr-aa, 'great house'
translationNotes.note: Pharaoh is a title, not a name. The Egyptian words behind it mean 'great house' and first named the palace itself, then came to stand for the man who lived in it, the way 'the White House' is used of a president. Exodus never gives the king a personal name; from 1:8 to the end he is 'Pharaoh' or 'the king of Egypt.' He was held to be a living god, the son of Ra, and responsible for holding the order of the world in place.

Fortified government depots for grain, oil, and weapons, not ordinary towns. Pithom and Rameses stood in the eastern Nile Delta; the site of Rameses, the Egyptian Pi-Ramesse, has been excavated at Qantir. Building them is what the forced labor of Exodus 1:11 was for.

Egyptian building brick was Nile mud mixed with chopped straw, pressed in a wooden mould and dried in the sun. The straw bound the clay and kept the brick from cracking as it shrank. That is why withholding straw in Exodus 5:7 while holding the quota was a punishment and not a saving.

Literally 'the two stones.' Egyptian women gave birth squatting or kneeling on a pair of bricks, and painted birth bricks of this kind have been recovered by excavation at Abydos. Pharaoh's order in Exodus 1:16 told the midwives to watch that moment and act on it.

The word outsiders use for Israel and the word Israelites use of themselves when talking to outsiders. Pharaoh calls them Hebrews at 1:15-16, Pharaoh's daughter says 'this is one of the Hebrew children' at 2:6, and Moses tells Pharaoh 'the God of the Hebrews' has sent him (7:16; 9:1). Abram carries the same label in Genesis 14:13, and Jonah answers a boatload of foreign sailors with 'I am a Hebrew' (Jonah 1:9).

The two midwives are named at 1:15 and the king who orders the killing never is. Their reply at 1:19 works because Egyptian and Israelite birth practice used the same equipment: they claim they simply arrive too late. Verse 21 records what they got for it, households of their own, which in that world meant descendants and a name that lasted.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jacob's descendants multiply greatly in Egypt until a new pharaoh enslaves them for forced labor; when he commands the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill all newborn boys, they refuse out of fear of God, so he orders the entire population to drown male infants in the Nile.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 2
summaryBullets: Now a man of the house of Levi married a Levite woman, (2:1).
and she conceived and gave birth to a son. When she saw that he was a beautiful child, she hid him for three months. (2:2).

But when she could no longer hide him, she got him a papyrus basket and coated it with tar and pitch. Then she placed the child in the basket and set it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile. (2:3).
And his sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him. (2:4).

Soon the daughter of Pharaoh went down to bathe in the Nile, and her attendants were walking along the riverbank. And when she saw the basket among the reeds, she sent her maidservant to retrieve it. (2:5).
When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the little boy was crying. So she had compassion on him and said, “This is one of the Hebrew children.” (2:6).
Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?” (2:7).
“Go ahead,” Pharaoh’s daughter told her. And the girl went and called the boy’s mother. (2:8).
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages.” So the woman took the boy and nursed him. (2:9).
When the child had grown older, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses and explained, “I drew him out of the water.” (2:10).
One day, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his own people and observed their hard labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people. (2:11).
After looking this way and that and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand. (2:12).
The next day Moses went out and saw two Hebrews fighting. He asked the one in the wrong, “Why are you attacking your companion?” (2:13).

But the man replied, “Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” Then Moses was afraid and thought, “This thing I have done has surely become known.” (2:14).
When Pharaoh heard about this matter, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian, where he sat down beside a well. (2:15).
Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father’s flock. (2:16).
And when some shepherds came along and drove them away, Moses rose up to help them and watered their flock. (2:17).
When the daughters returned to their father Reuel, he asked them, “Why have you returned so early today?” (2:18).
“An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds,” they replied. “He even drew water for us and watered the flock.” (2:19).
“So where is he?” their father asked. “Why did you leave the man behind? Invite him to have something to eat.” (2:20).
Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage. (2:21).
And she gave birth to a son, and Moses named him Gershom, saying, “I have become a foreigner in a foreign land.” (2:22).
After a long time, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned and cried out under their burden of slavery, and their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God. (2:23).
So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. (2:24).
God saw the Israelites and took notice. (2:25).
crossRefs: Genesis 6:14: Noah is told to build a tevah and coat it with pitch, the only other use of that word in the Hebrew Bible.
Hebrews 11:23-27: Moses' parents hid him three months, and Moses left Egypt without fearing the king's anger.
Acts 7:20-29: Stephen's account of Moses' first forty years, the Egyptian he struck down, and his flight to Midian.
Genesis 25:1-2: Midian is named as a son of Abraham by Keturah.
Exodus 18:1-12: Jethro the priest of Midian later brings Zipporah and her two sons back to Moses.

translationNotes.note: The word here is not the ordinary word for a basket. It is tevah, used in the Hebrew Bible only for this basket and for Noah's ark in Genesis 6:14, and both are sealed with pitch. English loses the link entirely by rendering one 'ark' and the other 'basket.'

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹשֶׁה (Mosheh) - from מָשָׁה (mashah), to draw out
translationNotes.note: Exodus 2:10 ties the name to the Hebrew verb mashah, to draw out. The same sounds carry an Egyptian sense as well: ms means 'is born' or 'son of,' and stands in royal names such as Ahmose and Thutmose. A boy raised in Pharaoh's house would have carried a name that worked in both languages.

The priest of Midian is called Reuel in Exodus 2:18 and Jethro from Exodus 3:1 onward. Reuel means 'friend of God' and Jethro means 'his excellence,' which reads as a personal name and a title. Numbers 10:29 names Hobab as his son.

Midian was a people and a territory, not a city. They descend from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2), so Moses marries into a branch of his own ancestor's family. Their range lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba in north-west Arabia and along the caravan roads, which is why Midianite traders are the ones carrying spices down to Egypt in Genesis 37:28. Numbers 22:4-7 and Judges 6:1-6 show the same people later as enemies.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּרְשֹׁם (Gershom), heard as גֵּר שָׁם (ger sham), 'a stranger there'
translationNotes.note: Moses explains the name himself at 2:22: he had become a foreigner in a foreign land. A ger is a resident alien, a man living where he holds no clan land and no clan protection. The whole law's insistence on treating the ger fairly, Exodus 22:21 and 23:9, is grounded on Israel having been one, and Moses names his firstborn for it.

stories.keyTakeaway: A Levite woman hides her newborn son in a basket on the Nile; Pharaoh's daughter finds him, names him Moses, and raises him as her own. Years later, after killing an Egyptian and fleeing to Midian, Moses marries Zipporah and settles there while Israel groans under slavery and God takes notice.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 3
summaryBullets: Meanwhile, Moses was shepherding the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. (3:1).
There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blazing fire from within a bush. Moses saw the bush ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed. (3:2).
So Moses thought, “I must go over and see this marvelous sight. Why is the bush not burning up?” (3:3).
When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called out to him from within the bush, “Moses, Moses!” “Here I am,” he answered. (3:4).
“Do not come any closer,” God said. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” (3:5).
Then He said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” At this, Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God. (3:6).
The LORD said, “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors, and I am aware of their sufferings. (3:7).

I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey— the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. (3:8).
And now the cry of the Israelites has reached Me, and I have seen how severely the Egyptians are oppressing them. (3:9).
Therefore, go! I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people the Israelites out of Egypt.” (3:10).
But Moses asked God, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” (3:11).
“I will surely be with you,” God said, “and this will be the sign to you that I have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, all of you will worship God on this mountain.” (3:12).
Then Moses asked God, “Suppose I go to the Israelites and say to them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is His name?’ What should I tell them?” (3:13).
God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” (3:14).

God also told Moses, “Say to the Israelites, ‘The LORD, the God of your fathers — the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob — has sent me to you.’ This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation. (3:15).

Go, assemble the elders of Israel and say to them, ‘The LORD, the God of your fathers — the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — has appeared to me and said: I have surely attended to you and have seen what has been done to you in Egypt. (3:16).

And I have promised to bring you up out of your affliction in Egypt, into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites— a land flowing with milk and honey.’ (3:17).

The elders of Israel will listen to what you say, and you must go with them to the king of Egypt and tell him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now please let us take a three-day journey into the wilderness, so that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.’ (3:18).
But I know that the king of Egypt will not allow you to go unless a mighty hand compels him. (3:19).
So I will stretch out My hand and strike the Egyptians with all the wonders I will perform among them. And after that, he will release you. (3:20).
And I will grant this people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that when you leave, you will not go away empty-handed. (3:21).

Every woman shall ask her neighbor and any woman staying in her house for silver and gold jewelry and clothing, and you will put them on your sons and daughters. So you will plunder the Egyptians.” (3:22).
crossRefs: Acts 7:30-34: Stephen recounts the angel in the burning bush at Sinai and the voice that sent Moses back to Egypt.
Mark 12:26-27: Jesus cites God's words at the bush to prove that the dead are raised.
John 8:58: Jesus tells the crowd, Before Abraham was born, I am.
Joshua 5:15: The commander of the LORD's army tells Joshua to take off his sandals, for the place is holy.
Exodus 6:2-8: God repeats the name and lays out the sevenfold promise to bring Israel out.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה (ehyeh asher ehyeh) - Greek (LXX): ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν (ego eimi ho on)
translationNotes.note: Moses asks for a name to give the elders and gets a sentence built on the verb 'to be' (3:14). Ehyeh is the ordinary first-person form, 'I am' or 'I will be'; the same verb stands behind the four letters YHWH, which 3:15 then gives as the name to use, with 'this is My name forever.' The Greek Old Testament turns it into a participle, 'the One who is.' English Bibles print that name as LORD in capitals, so the reader sees a title where the Hebrew has a name.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָבַד (avad), to serve or to work
translationNotes.note: The sign God gives Moses at 3:12 is that Israel will serve God on this mountain, and the verb is the same one used at 1:13-14 for the slave labour they are serving Egypt under. The whole contest is over which master they work for, which is why the demand to Pharaoh is 'let My people go, so that they may serve Me' (7:16; 8:1; 9:1; 10:3). English splits one Hebrew verb into 'serve' when Egypt is the master and 'worship' when God is.

Horeb and Sinai name the same mountain; Exodus 3:1 calls it Horeb and Exodus 19:11 calls it Sinai. Moses was pasturing a flock there, which means it lay within reach of Midianite grazing east of the Gulf of Aqaba. The text calls it 'the mountain of God' before anything happens on it.

A description of pastoral wealth, not of a land of dessert. Milk means flocks and herds enough to keep producing it, and devash covers both bee honey and the thick syrup boiled down from dates and grapes. The phrase promises land good enough to graze and to farm.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים (derekh sheloshet yamim)
translationNotes.note: A standard ancient distance reckoning: as far as a group with flocks could walk in three days, roughly 45 to 60 miles. Moses asks Pharaoh for exactly this in Exodus 3:18 and repeats it in Exodus 5:3 and 8:27. It puts Israel beyond the settled Delta and its Egyptian garrisons.

Seneh is a thorny desert bush, and the word appears in Scripture only in this scene and in Deuteronomy 33:16, which blesses Joseph with the favour of the One who dwelt in the bush. It is not a tree and not remarkable; the point at 3:2-3 is that the fire keeps burning and the bush is not consumed, which is what makes Moses turn aside to look.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses encounters God in a burning bush at Horeb; God reveals himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, tells Moses he has seen Israel's suffering in Egypt, and commissions Moses to bring the people out to the land of Canaan. God gives Moses his name - I AM WHO I AM - instructs him to gather the elders and approach Pharaoh, and promises to strike Egypt with wonders so the people will be released and leave with plunder.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 4
summaryBullets: Then Moses answered, “What if they do not believe me or listen to my voice? For they may say, ‘The LORD has not appeared to you.’” (4:1).
And the LORD asked him, “What is that in your hand?” “A staff,” he replied. (4:2).
“Throw it on the ground,” said the LORD. So Moses threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and he ran from it. (4:3).
“Stretch out your hand and grab it by the tail,” the LORD said to Moses, who reached out his hand and caught the snake, and it turned back into a staff in his hand. (4:4).
“This is so that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers — the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob — has appeared to you.” (4:5).
Furthermore, the LORD said to Moses, “Put your hand inside your cloak.” So he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, his hand was leprous, white as snow. (4:6).
“Put your hand back inside your cloak,” said the LORD. So Moses put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, it was restored, like the rest of his skin. (4:7).
And the LORD said, “If they refuse to believe you or heed the witness of the first sign, they may believe that of the second. (4:8).

But if they do not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground. Then the water you take from the Nile will become blood on the ground.” (4:9).
“Please, Lord,” Moses replied, “I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since You have spoken to Your servant, for I am slow of speech and tongue.” (4:10).
And the LORD said to him, “Who gave man his mouth? Or who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD? (4:11).
Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.” (4:12).
But Moses replied, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” (4:13).

Then the anger of the LORD burned against Moses, and He said, “Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he can speak well, and he is now on his way to meet you. When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart. (4:14).
You are to speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will help both of you to speak, and I will teach you what to do. (4:15).
He will speak to the people for you. He will be your spokesman, and it will be as if you were God to him. (4:16).
But take this staff in your hand so you can perform signs with it.” (4:17).
Then Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said to him, “Please let me return to my brothers in Egypt to see if they are still alive.” “Go in peace,” Jethro replied. (4:18).
Now the LORD had said to Moses in Midian, “Go back to Egypt, for all the men who sought to kill you are dead.” (4:19).
So Moses took his wife and sons, put them on a donkey, and headed back to Egypt. And he took the staff of God in his hand. (4:20).

The LORD instructed Moses, “When you go back to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders that I have put within your power. But I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go. (4:21).
Then tell Pharaoh that this is what the LORD says: ‘Israel is My firstborn son, (4:22).
and I told you to let My son go so that he may worship Me. But since you have refused to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son!’” (4:23).
Now at a lodging place along the way, the LORD met Moses and was about to kill him. (4:24).
But Zipporah took a flint knife, cut off her son’s foreskin, and touched it to Moses’ feet. “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me,” she said. (4:25).
So the LORD let him alone. (When she said, “bridegroom of blood,” she was referring to the circumcision.) (4:26).
Meanwhile, the LORD had said to Aaron, “Go and meet Moses in the wilderness.” So he went and met Moses at the mountain of God and kissed him. (4:27).
And Moses told Aaron everything the LORD had sent him to say, and all the signs He had commanded him to perform. (4:28).
Then Moses and Aaron went and assembled all the elders of the Israelites, (4:29).
and Aaron relayed everything the LORD had said to Moses. And Moses performed the signs before the people, (4:30).
and they believed. And when they heard that the LORD had attended to the Israelites and had seen their affliction, they bowed down and worshiped. (4:31).
crossRefs: Acts 7:35-36: The man Israel rejected was sent as ruler and deliverer, working wonders in Egypt and at the Red Sea.
Hosea 11:1: When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son.
Genesis 17:9-14: Circumcision commanded as the sign of the covenant, and the uncircumcised cut off from his people.
Jeremiah 1:6-9: Jeremiah protests that he cannot speak, and the LORD puts His words in his mouth.
Exodus 7:1-2: God makes Moses like God to Pharaoh and Aaron his prophet.

translationNotes.note: A different verb from the 'serve' of 3:12. Shachah is physical: to go down face-first before someone. It is used of Abraham before the three visitors (Genesis 18:2) and before the Hittites (Genesis 23:7), so it covers ordinary respect to a superior as well as reverence to God. At 4:31 the people hear that God has seen their misery and go down on their faces.

At 4:22-23 God tells Moses to call Israel 'My firstborn son' and to warn Pharaoh that refusing to let him go will cost Pharaoh his own firstborn. The firstborn son held the headship of the family and a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17). The warning is delivered before the first plague and collected in 12:29, and 13:2 then claims every firstborn in Israel for God on the strength of it.

The Hebrew tsaraat covers a range of skin conditions, not the modern disease named after Hansen. Leviticus 13 sets out the priest's inspection for it in detail. The sign given to Moses runs the condition forward and back inside a single verse.

Circumcision was performed with a knapped stone blade long after metal was common; Joshua 5:2 uses flint knives at Gilgal for the same rite. A fresh flint edge is sharper than bronze and can be made on the spot. Zipporah acts with what was at hand at a lodging place.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּבַד־פֶּה וּכְבַד לָשׁוֹן (kevad-peh u-khevad lashon)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue.' The same root kaved describes Pharaoh's heavy heart a few verses later in Exodus 4:21, so the book uses one word for the prophet's difficulty and the king's obstinacy. English splits them into 'slow' and 'hardened.'

stories.keyTakeaway: God gives Moses three signs to prove his authority to the Israelites - a staff turning into a snake, a hand becoming leprous and then healed, and water turning to blood - and provides Aaron as his spokesman when Moses resists. Moses returns to Egypt with his family and staff; Aaron meets him in the wilderness, they gather the elders, perform the signs, and the people believe and worship.

headings.text: The People Believe Moses and Aaron

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 5
summaryBullets: After that, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.’” (5:1).
But Pharaoh replied, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.” (5:2).

“The God of the Hebrews has met with us,” they answered. “Please let us go on a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD our God, or He may strike us with plagues or with the sword.” (5:3).
But the king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why do you draw the people away from their work? Get back to your labor!” (5:4).
Pharaoh also said, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.” (5:5).
That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen: (5:6).
“You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks. They must go and gather their own straw. (5:7).
But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it. For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’ (5:8).
Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies.” (5:9).
So the taskmasters and foremen of the people went out and said to them, “This is what Pharaoh says: ‘I am no longer giving you straw. (5:10).
Go and get your own straw wherever you can find it; but your workload will in no way be reduced.’” (5:11).
So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw. (5:12).
The taskmasters kept pressing them, saying, “Fulfill your quota each day, just as you did when straw was provided.” (5:13).
Then the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over the people, were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?” (5:14).
So the Israelite foremen went and appealed to Pharaoh: “Why are you treating your servants this way? (5:15).
No straw has been given to your servants, yet we are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” (5:16).
“You are slackers!” Pharaoh replied. “Slackers! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’ (5:17).
Now get to work. You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.” (5:18).
The Israelite foremen realized they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks.” (5:19).
When they left Pharaoh, they confronted Moses and Aaron, who stood waiting to meet them. (5:20).
“May the LORD look upon you and judge you,” the foremen said, “for you have made us a stench before Pharaoh and his officials; you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!” (5:21).
So Moses returned to the LORD and asked, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me? (5:22).
Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and You have not delivered Your people in any way.” (5:23).
crossRefs: Exodus 1:11-14: The taskmasters and the brick labor first imposed on Israel.
Exodus 6:6-9: God answers the failed first appeal with the promise to redeem Israel with an outstretched arm.
Deuteronomy 26:6-7: The Egyptians treated us harshly and imposed hard labor, and we cried out to the LORD.
Psalm 81:6: I removed the burden from his shoulder; his hands were freed from the basket.
Numbers 11:11-15: Moses again asks the LORD why He has laid the burden of this people on him.

translationNotes.note: Two different ranks. The nogsim were Egyptian drivers who set the quota; the shoterim were Israelite foremen made responsible for meeting it, and in Exodus 5:14 they are the ones beaten when it is missed. Making the oppressed police the oppressed was standard Egyptian labor administration.

Teven is threshed straw, cut and stored for use. Qash is stubble, the stalk left standing in the field after harvest, which had to be pulled up by hand. Exodus 5:12 has Israel scattered across Egypt gathering the worse material while the brick quota stayed the same.

translationNotes.term: who is the LORD, that I should obey Him
translationNotes.note: Pharaoh's question in Exodus 5:2 is not simple defiance. In Egyptian religion the king was himself divine: the living Horus, the son of Ra, and the man personally responsible for holding the order of the world in place. Temple walls show him alone making offerings to the gods, and the crown he wore carried the rearing cobra of the goddess Wadjet. So a demand delivered in the name of a god he had never heard of, on behalf of slaves, was a challenge to his own standing, which is why Exodus 12:12 states the contest as one against the gods of Egypt.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַג (chag), from חָגַג (chagag), to make pilgrimage
translationNotes.note: The request at 5:1 is not for a day off. A chag is a pilgrim festival: you travel to it, and Exodus 23:14-17 names the three Israel must keep every year. The same root survives in the Arabic hajj. Pharaoh hears a demand that his entire labour force walk three days out of the country to hold one, which is why 5:4-9 answers it by raising the work rate.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go worship in the wilderness, but Pharaoh refuses, dismisses the God of Israel, and instead increases the Israelites' labor by requiring them to gather their own straw while maintaining the same brick quota. The overseers are beaten, appeal to Pharaoh without success, and then blame Moses and Aaron for making their situation worse.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 6
summaryBullets: But the LORD said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh, for because of My mighty hand he will let the people go; because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.” (6:1).
God also told Moses, “I am the LORD. (6:2).
I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them. (6:3).
I also established My covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners. (6:4).
Furthermore, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered My covenant. (6:5).

Therefore tell the Israelites: ‘I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians and deliver you from their bondage. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment. (6:6).
I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians. (6:7).
And I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD!’” (6:8).
Moses relayed this message to the Israelites, but on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage, they did not listen to him. (6:9).
So the LORD said to Moses, (6:10).
“Go and tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the Israelites go out of his land.” (6:11).
But in the LORD’s presence Moses replied, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, then why would Pharaoh listen to me, since I am unskilled in speech?” (6:12).
Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge concerning both the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt. (6:13).
These were the heads of their fathers’ houses: The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel, were Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. These were the clans of Reuben. (6:14).
The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These were the clans of Simeon. (6:15).
These were the names of the sons of Levi according to their records: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years. (6:16).
The sons of Gershon were Libni and Shimei, by their clans. (6:17).
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived 133 years. (6:18).
The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. These were the clans of the Levites according to their records. (6:19).
And Amram married his father’s sister Jochebed, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. Amram lived 137 years. (6:20).
The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri. (6:21).
The sons of Uzziel were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri. (6:22).
And Aaron married Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. (6:23).
The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These were the clans of the Korahites. (6:24).
Aaron’s son Eleazar married one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These were the heads of the Levite families by their clans. (6:25).
It was this Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, “Bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.” (6:26).
Moses and Aaron were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt in order to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. (6:27).
Now on the day that the LORD spoke to Moses in Egypt, (6:28).
He said to him, “I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I say to you.” (6:29).
But in the LORD’s presence Moses replied, “Since I am unskilled in speech, why would Pharaoh listen to me?” (6:30).
crossRefs: Exodus 3:13-15: God first gives the name by which He is to be remembered in every generation.
Genesis 17:1-8: God appears to Abram as God Almighty and grants the land of Canaan to his offspring.
Numbers 3:17-20: The same Levite line of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, organized for tabernacle service.
1 Chronicles 6:1-15: The priestly line traced from Levi through Aaron down to the exile.
Ezekiel 20:5-9: The LORD recalls making Himself known to Israel in Egypt and swearing to bring them out.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צְבָאוֹת (tsevaot), armies or organised divisions
translationNotes.note: Israel does not straggle out of Egypt; the text keeps saying they went out by their tsevaot, their divisions, at 6:26, 7:4, 12:41 and 12:51. Tsava is the ordinary word for an army in the field and for a term of military service (Numbers 1:3). The census in Numbers 1 is a muster of exactly these divisions, and the camp of Numbers 2 is laid out as a marching order.

The name by which God dealt with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, used in Genesis 17:1, 28:3, and 35:11. Exodus 6:3 contrasts it with the covenant name given to Moses. 'Almighty' comes through the Greek and Latin versions; the Hebrew root is not settled, and the text does not define it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּרְשׁוֹן, קְהָת, מְרָרִי (Gershon, Qehat, Merari)
translationNotes.note: Levi's three sons head the three Levite work groups. Numbers 3 and 4 assign each a share of the tabernacle: Kohathites carry the holy furniture, Gershonites the curtains and coverings, Merarites the frames, bars, and bases. Moses and Aaron come from Kohath through Amram.

translationNotes.term: I will bring, deliver, redeem, take
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְהוֹצֵאתִי, וְהִצַּלְתִּי, וְגָאַלְתִּי, וְלָקַחְתִּי (vehotseti, vehitsalti, vega alti, velaqachti)
translationNotes.note: Four verbs in 6:6-7 set out the whole rescue in order: bring out from under the burdens, deliver from the slavery, redeem with an outstretched arm, take as His own people. Ga al, to redeem, is the family word: it is what a kinsman does when he buys back a relative's land or a relative himself (Leviticus 25:47-49), and it is the word behind Boaz in Ruth 4. The Mishnah, compiled about 200 AD, requires four cups of wine at the Passover meal (Pesachim 10:1); the Jerusalem Talmud connects those four cups to these four verbs.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲרַל שְׂפָתַיִם (aral sefatayim), literally 'uncircumcised of lips'
translationNotes.note: Moses' objection at 6:12 and again at 6:30 uses the same word Israel uses for an uncircumcised man, applied to his mouth. Hebrew stretches it further: Jeremiah 6:10 speaks of an uncircumcised ear that cannot listen, and Leviticus 26:41 of an uncircumcised heart. In each case it means the thing is closed off and will not do its job.

stories.keyTakeaway: God promises Moses he will free the Israelites from Egypt by his mighty hand and bring them to Canaan; Moses reports this to the discouraged Israelites who don't listen, then objects that Pharaoh won't listen to him either. The chapter then lists the genealogies of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, identifying Aaron and Moses as the ones God commands to bring Israel out of Egypt.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 7
summaryBullets: The LORD answered Moses, “See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet. (7:1).
You are to speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go out of his land. (7:2).
But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and though I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, (7:3).
Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay My hand on Egypt, and by mighty acts of judgment I will bring the divisions of My people the Israelites out of the land of Egypt. (7:4).
And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them.” (7:5).
So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them. (7:6).
Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh. (7:7).
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, (7:8).
“When Pharaoh tells you, ‘Perform a miracle,’ you are to say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh,’ and it will become a serpent.” (7:9).
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD had commanded. Aaron threw his staff down before Pharaoh and his officials, and it became a serpent. (7:10).
But Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt, and they also did the same things by their magic arts. (7:11).
Each one threw down his staff, and it became a serpent. But Aaron’s staff swallowed up the other staffs. (7:12).
Still, Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said. (7:13).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is unyielding; he refuses to let the people go. (7:14).
Go to Pharaoh in the morning as you see him walking out to the water. Wait on the bank of the Nile to meet him, and take in your hand the staff that was changed into a snake. (7:15).
Then say to him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to tell you: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness. But until now you have not listened. (7:16).
This is what the LORD says: By this you will know that I am the LORD. Behold, with the staff in my hand I will strike the water of the Nile, and it will turn to blood. (7:17).
The fish in the Nile will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will be unable to drink its water.’” (7:18).

And the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt— over their rivers and canals and ponds and all the reservoirs— that they may become blood.’ There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in the vessels of wood and stone.” (7:19).

Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded; in the presence of Pharaoh and his officials, Aaron raised the staff and struck the water of the Nile, and all the water was turned to blood. (7:20).
The fish in the Nile died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink its water. And there was blood throughout the land of Egypt. (7:21).
But the magicians of Egypt did the same things by their magic arts. So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said. (7:22).
Instead, Pharaoh turned around, went into his palace, and did not take any of this to heart. (7:23).
So all the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink the water from the river. (7:24).
And seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile. (7:25).
crossRefs: Exodus 4:2-9: The staff, the leprous hand, and Nile water turned to blood given to Moses as signs.
2 Timothy 3:8-9: Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, and their folly became plain to everyone.
Psalm 105:29: He turned their waters into blood and caused their fish to die.
Isaiah 19:5-8: The Nile dries up, the canals stink, and the fishermen of Egypt mourn.
Revelation 16:3-4: Bowls of wrath turn the sea and the rivers to blood.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָשָׁה (qashah), to make hard - חָזַק (chazaq), to make strong - כָּבֵד (kaved), to be heavy
translationNotes.note: Three different Hebrew verbs arrive in English as one word. At 7:3 God says He will make Pharaoh's heart qasheh, hard; at 7:13 it is chazaq, strong or firm; at 7:14 it is kaved, heavy, the same root as the 'heavy' labour of 5:9 and the 'heavy' mouth Moses complained of at 4:10. The text distributes the action as well as the vocabulary: Pharaoh hardens his own heart at 8:15, 8:32 and 9:34, and the LORD is named as the one hardening it from 9:12 on.

A loanword from Egyptian, describing the lector priests who read the ritual books and were credited with power over nature. They are court professionals, not stage entertainers. 2 Timothy 3:8 names two of them, Jannes and Jambres.

Exodus 4:3 turns the staff into a nachash, an ordinary snake. Before Pharaoh in Exodus 7:9 the word changes to tannin, the term for the great creatures of Genesis 1:21, and the word Ezekiel 29:3 uses for Pharaoh himself, the monster lying in his own streams. English prints 'snake' and 'serpent' and the change disappears.

The Hebrew uses an Egyptian loanword for the river, not the usual word for a stream. Egypt's whole food supply depended on the Nile flood, and the inundation was worshipped as the god Hapi. Exodus 12:12 states that the LORD executed judgment against all the gods of Egypt, and the first blow lands on the river.

Verse 7:7 dates the confrontation precisely: Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three when they walk into the throne room. Acts 7:23 and 7:30 divide his life into forty in Egypt and forty in Midian, and Deuteronomy 34:7 puts him at a hundred and twenty when he dies, which makes the wilderness the last forty.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD instructs Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh; Aaron's staff becomes a snake and swallows the staffs of Pharaoh's magicians, but Pharaoh's heart hardens. Moses then strikes the Nile with his staff and turns all the water to blood throughout Egypt, yet Pharaoh's magicians replicate the act and Pharaoh refuses to listen.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 8
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. (8:1).
But if you refuse to let them go, I will plague your whole country with frogs. (8:2).

The Nile will teem with frogs, and they will come into your palace and up to your bedroom and onto your bed, into the houses of your officials and your people, and into your ovens and kneading bowls. (8:3).
The frogs will come up on you and your people and all your officials.’” (8:4).
And the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers and canals and ponds, and cause the frogs to come up onto the land of Egypt.’” (8:5).
So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. (8:6).
But the magicians did the same thing by their magic arts, and they also brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt. (8:7).
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people. Then I will let your people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD.” (8:8).

Moses said to Pharaoh, “You may have the honor over me. When shall I pray for you and your officials and your people that the frogs (except for those in the Nile) may be taken away from you and your houses?” (8:9).
“Tomorrow,” Pharaoh answered. “May it be as you say,” Moses replied, “so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God. (8:10).
The frogs will depart from you and your houses and your officials and your people; they will remain only in the Nile.” (8:11).
After Moses and Aaron had left Pharaoh, Moses cried out to the LORD for help with the frogs that He had brought against Pharaoh. (8:12).
And the LORD did as Moses requested, and the frogs in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields died. (8:13).
They were piled into countless heaps, and there was a terrible stench in the land. (8:14).
When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, however, he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said. (8:15).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, that it may turn into swarms of gnats throughout the land of Egypt.’” (8:16).

This they did, and when Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, gnats came upon man and beast. All the dust of the earth turned into gnats throughout the land of Egypt. (8:17).
The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not. And the gnats remained on man and beast. (8:18).
“This is the finger of God,” the magicians said to Pharaoh. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said. (8:19).

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Get up early in the morning, and when Pharaoh goes out to the water, stand before him and tell him that this is what the LORD says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. (8:20).

But if you will not let My people go, I will send swarms of flies upon you and your officials and your people and your houses. The houses of the Egyptians and even the ground where they stand will be full of flies. (8:21).
But on that day I will give special treatment to the land of Goshen, where My people live; no swarms of flies will be found there. In this way you will know that I, the LORD, am in the land. (8:22).
I will make a distinction between My people and your people. This sign will take place tomorrow.’” (8:23).
And the LORD did so. Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh’s palace and into the houses of his officials. Throughout Egypt the land was ruined by swarms of flies. (8:24).
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Go, sacrifice to your God within this land.” (8:25).

But Moses replied, “It would not be right to do that, because the sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God would be detestable to the Egyptians. If we offer sacrifices that are detestable before the Egyptians, will they not stone us? (8:26).
We must make a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as He commands us.” (8:27).
Pharaoh answered, “I will let you go and sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far. Now pray for me.” (8:28).

“As soon as I leave you,” Moses said, “I will pray to the LORD, so that tomorrow the swarms of flies will depart from Pharaoh and his officials and his people. But Pharaoh must not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go and sacrifice to the LORD.” (8:29).
Then Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD, (8:30).
and the LORD did as Moses requested. He removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh and his officials and his people; not one fly remained. (8:31).
But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well, and he would not let the people go. (8:32).
crossRefs: Psalm 105:30-31: Their land teemed with frogs, and swarms of flies and gnats filled their territory.
Psalm 78:45: He sent swarms of flies that devoured them and frogs that devastated them.
Luke 11:20: Jesus says that if He drives out demons by the finger of God, the kingdom of God has come.
Exodus 11:7: The LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel, so that not even a dog will snarl.
Revelation 16:13: Three unclean spirits like frogs come out of the mouth of the dragon.

translationNotes.note: Frogs bred in the Nile mud after the flood receded, and the Egyptians worshipped a frog-headed goddess, Heqet, who was invoked at childbirth. Exodus 8:3 puts them in the ovens and kneading bowls, which under Egyptian purity rules made the household food unusable.

Small biting insects, rendered gnats, lice, or mosquitoes. The detail that matters is in Exodus 8:18: the lector priests could not reproduce this one. Egyptian priests shaved their whole bodies and bathed repeatedly to stay ritually clean, and a plague of body vermin shut their service down.

The magicians' own phrase in Exodus 8:19, conceding a power they cannot copy. The same expression describes the writing of the tablets in Exodus 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10. Jesus uses it in Luke 11:20.

Pharaoh offers a compromise in Exodus 8:25: worship, but do it inside Egypt. Moses refuses on a practical ground at 8:26, that the sacrifices would be detestable to the Egyptians and the people would stone them for it. Egypt held certain animals sacred, cattle above all, and Genesis 46:34 has already said that every shepherd is detestable to Egyptians. Killing bulls and rams in public view of an Egyptian town was not a religious nicety; it would have started a riot.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרֹב (arov), from a root meaning to mix or swarm
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word names a swarm and does not say of what; 'flies' is supplied by translators. The Greek Old Testament chose kunomuia, the dog-fly, a biting fly of the region. Verse 8:24 says the land was ruined by them, which fits an insect that torments livestock and people rather than one that merely annoys.

The district in the eastern Nile Delta where Joseph settled his family (Genesis 47:6, 11), good grazing land on the edge of Egypt rather than in its heart. From this plague on, the text keeps drawing a line at its border: no swarms in Goshen (8:22), no hail in Goshen (9:26). The separation is the point being made, and 8:23 says so.

stories.keyTakeaway: God sends frogs, gnats, and flies as plagues on Egypt; Pharaoh repeatedly agrees to release Israel when the plagues strike, then hardens his heart and refuses once the plagues lift.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 9
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. (9:1).
But if you continue to restrain them and refuse to let them go, (9:2).
then the hand of the LORD will bring a severe plague on your livestock in the field— on your horses, donkeys, camels, herds, and flocks. (9:3).
But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that no animal belonging to the Israelites will die.’” (9:4).
The LORD set a time, saying, “Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land.” (9:5).
And the next day the LORD did just that. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one animal belonging to the Israelites died. (9:6).
Pharaoh sent officials and found that none of the livestock of the Israelites had died. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go. (9:7).
Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of soot from the furnace; in the sight of Pharaoh, Moses is to toss it into the air. (9:8).
It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and festering boils will break out on man and beast throughout the land.” (9:9).
So they took soot from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh. Moses tossed it into the air, and festering boils broke out on man and beast. (9:10).
The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians. (9:11).
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses. (9:12).

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Get up early in the morning, stand before Pharaoh, and tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. (9:13).
Otherwise, I will send all My plagues against you and your officials and your people, so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth. (9:14).
For by this time I could have stretched out My hand and struck you and your people with a plague to wipe you off the earth. (9:15).
But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth. (9:16).
Still, you lord it over My people and do not allow them to go. (9:17).
Behold, at this time tomorrow I will rain down the worst hail that has ever fallen on Egypt, from the day it was founded until now. (9:18).

So give orders now to shelter your livestock and everything you have in the field. Every man or beast that remains in the field and is not brought inside will die when the hail comes down upon them.’” (9:19).
Those among Pharaoh’s officials who feared the word of the LORD hurried to bring their servants and livestock to shelter, (9:20).
but those who disregarded the word of the LORD left their servants and livestock in the field. (9:21).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that hail may fall on all the land of Egypt— on man and beast and every plant of the field throughout the land of Egypt.” (9:22).
So Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth. So the LORD rained down hail upon the land of Egypt. (9:23).
The hail fell and the lightning continued flashing through it. The hail was so severe that nothing like it had ever been seen in all the land of Egypt from the time it became a nation. (9:24).
Throughout the land of Egypt, the hail struck down everything in the field, both man and beast; it beat down every plant of the field and stripped every tree. (9:25).
The only place where it did not hail was in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived. (9:26).
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. “This time I have sinned,” he said. “The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked. (9:27).
Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail. I will let you go; you do not need to stay any longer.” (9:28).

Moses said to him, “When I have left the city, I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s. (9:29).
But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God.” (9:30).
(Now the flax and barley were destroyed, since the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom; (9:31).
but the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops.) (9:32).
Then Moses departed from Pharaoh, went out of the city, and spread out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured down on the land. (9:33).
When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart — he and his officials. (9:34).
So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the Israelites go, just as the LORD had said through Moses. (9:35).
crossRefs: Psalm 78:47-48: He destroyed their vines with hail and their herds with lightning bolts.
Psalm 105:32-33: He gave them hail for rain, with lightning throughout their land, and shattered their trees.
Romans 9:17: Paul quotes the word spoken to Pharaoh, I raised you up to display My power in you.
Deuteronomy 28:27: The boils of Egypt are listed among the curses for covenant breaking.
Revelation 16:21: Enormous hailstones fall from heaven on men, and they curse God.

translationNotes.note: The word covers herds and flocks as property and wealth. Egypt kept sacred bulls, Apis at Memphis and Mnevis at Heliopolis, and the cow goddess Hathor was among the most widely worshipped deities in the land. Exodus 9:4 records that the plague drew a line between Israel's animals and Egypt's.

Ash from a brick kiln, the very furnace Israel had been forced to work. Thrown into the air it became festering boils on man and beast. The lector priests could not even stand before Moses because the boils were on them too (Exodus 9:11).

translationNotes.term: flax and barley, wheat and spelt
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פִּשְׁתָּה וּשְׂעֹרָה (pishtah u-seorah) - חִטָּה וְכֻסֶּמֶת (chittah u-khussemet)
translationNotes.note: This is a dated agricultural note dropped into the narrative. Barley ripens about a month ahead of wheat, and flax is pulled while in flower. Exodus 9:31-32 says the barley was already in the ear and the flax in bloom while the wheat and spelt were still green, which places the hail a few weeks before the Exodus in the month of Abib.

Dever is the standard word for an epidemic, used of both animals and people, and it turns up in the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:21 and in David's choice at 2 Samuel 24:13-15. Here at 9:3 it falls on horses, donkeys, camels, cattle and flocks, which is to say on Egypt's transport, its ploughing, and its meat and milk at once.

translationNotes.term: the officials who feared the word
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַיָּרֵא אֶת־דְּבַר יְהוָה (hayyare et-devar YHWH)
translationNotes.note: Verses 9:20-21 split Pharaoh's own court in two. Some officials believed the warning and brought their slaves and animals under cover before the hail; others left them in the field and lost them. It is the first sign in the account that the warnings were landing on Egyptians, and 12:38 records that a mixed crowd left the country with Israel.

stories.keyTakeaway: God sends a plague killing all Egyptian livestock while sparing Israel's, then a plague of boils on people and animals; when Pharaoh still refuses to release Israel, God sends a devastating hailstorm that destroys crops and kills anyone caught outside, though it avoids Goshen. Pharaoh temporarily agrees to let Israel go after the hail stops, but immediately hardens his heart again and refuses.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 10
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his officials, that I may perform these miraculous signs of Mine among them, (10:1).
and that you may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians when I performed miraculous signs among them, so that all of you may know that I am the LORD.” (10:2).

So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and told him, “This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me? Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. (10:3).
But if you refuse to let My people go, I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow. (10:4).
They will cover the face of the land so that no one can see it. They will devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields. (10:5).

They will fill your houses and the houses of all your officials and every Egyptian— something neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen since the day they came into this land.’” Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh’s presence. (10:6).
Pharaoh’s officials asked him, “How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God. Do you not yet realize that Egypt lies in ruins?” (10:7).
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. “Go, worship the LORD your God,” he said. “But who exactly will be going?” (10:8).
“We will go with our young and old,” Moses replied. “We will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD.” (10:9).
Then Pharaoh told them, “May the LORD be with you if I ever let you go with your little ones. Clearly you are bent on evil. (10:10).
No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting.” And Moses and Aaron were driven from Pharaoh’s presence. (10:11).

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, so that the locusts may swarm over it and devour every plant in the land — everything that the hail has left behind.” (10:12).
So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and throughout that day and night the LORD sent an east wind across the land. By morning the east wind had brought the locusts. (10:13).
The locusts swarmed across the land and settled over the entire territory of Egypt. Never before had there been so many locusts, and never again will there be. (10:14).

They covered the face of all the land until it was black, and they consumed all the plants on the ground and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left behind. Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt. (10:15).
Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you. (10:16).
Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me.” (10:17).
So Moses left Pharaoh’s presence and appealed to the LORD. (10:18).
And the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt. (10:19).
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not let the Israelites go. (10:20).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that darkness may spread over the land of Egypt — a palpable darkness.” (10:21).
So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days. (10:22).
No one could see anyone else, and for three days no one left his place. Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings. (10:23).
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, “Go, worship the LORD. Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind.” (10:24).
But Moses replied, “You must also provide us with sacrifices and burnt offerings to present to the LORD our God. (10:25).

Even our livestock must go with us; not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God, and we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive.” (10:26).
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was unwilling to let them go. (10:27).
“Depart from me!” Pharaoh said to Moses. “Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die.” (10:28).
“As you say,” Moses replied, “I will never see your face again.” (10:29).
crossRefs: Joel 1:4-7: A locust swarm strips the land, leaving the fig trees bare and the branches white.
Psalm 105:34-35: He spoke, and locusts came without number and devoured every plant in the land.
Joel 2:1-2: A day of darkness and gloom, like blackness spread over the mountains.
Deuteronomy 6:20-25: When your son asks what these statutes mean, you are to tell him you were slaves in Egypt.
Revelation 16:10: The fifth bowl plunges the kingdom of the beast into darkness.

translationNotes.note: The desert locust, which swarms and migrates on the wind; Exodus 10:13 brings them on an east wind and Exodus 10:19 clears them on a west one. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization reckons a swarm covering one square kilometer holds about 40 million insects and eats in a day what 35,000 people would eat. The text says nothing green was left in Egypt.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְיָמֵשׁ חֹשֶׁךְ (ve-yamesh choshekh), 'darkness that may be felt'
translationNotes.note: The verb means to grope or to feel with the hand. Egypt's chief deity was the sun god Ra, and Pharaoh held his throne as Ra's son, so the sun going out for three days struck at the crown as well as the temple. Exodus 10:23 notes that Israel had light where they lived.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָבְדָה מִצְרָיִם (avedah Mitsrayim), 'Egypt is destroyed'
translationNotes.note: At 10:7 Pharaoh's own officials tell him the country is finished and ask him to let the people go, before the locusts have even arrived. The plagues have already taken the river, the livestock, and the barley and flax harvest (9:31), and the court can read a ledger. It is the second time in the book that Egyptians break with their king, after 9:20.

Pharaoh negotiates three times and each offer keeps a hostage. Sacrifice inside Egypt (8:25); go, but not far (8:28); only the men, leaving wives and children behind (10:11); and finally everyone but the flocks and herds (10:24). Moses refuses each in turn, and answers the last one at 10:26 with 'not a hoof will be left behind,' because the animals are what the sacrifices are made of.

The locusts arrive on an east wind (10:13) and leave on a west one (10:19), which is how desert locust swarms actually travel: they ride the prevailing wind rather than steering. The same east wind drives back the sea at 14:21. Hebrew uses one word, ruach, for wind, breath and spirit, so the reader of the original hears the same word in all three places.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses warns Pharaoh of a locust plague; when it devastates Egypt, Pharaoh asks forgiveness, but after the locusts are blown away he hardens his heart again. The LORD then brings three days of darkness over Egypt, and when Pharaoh offers to let the Israelites go but retain their livestock, Moses refuses and Pharaoh orders him never to return.

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 11
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, “I will bring upon Pharaoh and Egypt one more plague. After that, he will allow you to leave this place. And when he lets you go, he will drive you out completely. (11:1).
Now announce to the people that men and women alike should ask their neighbors for articles of silver and gold.” (11:2).
And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, Moses himself was highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people. (11:3).
So Moses declared, “This is what the LORD says: ‘About midnight I will go throughout Egypt, (11:4).

and every firstborn son in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill, as well as the firstborn of all the cattle. (11:5).
Then a great cry will go out over all the land of Egypt. Such an outcry has never been heard before and will never be heard again. (11:6).
But among all the Israelites, not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.’ Then you will know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel. (11:7).

And all these officials of yours will come and bow before me, saying, ‘Go, you and all the people who follow you!’ After that, I will depart.” And hot with anger, Moses left Pharaoh’s presence. (11:8).
The LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.” (11:9).
Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that he would not let the Israelites go out of his land. (11:10).
crossRefs: Exodus 12:29-30: The announcement carried out at midnight, with loud wailing in every Egyptian house.
Psalm 78:51: He struck down all the firstborn of Egypt, the firstfruits of their virility in the tents of Ham.
Psalm 136:10: To Him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, for His loving devotion endures forever.
Exodus 3:21-22: God promises Israel will not go away empty-handed but will plunder the Egyptians.
Hebrews 11:28: By faith Moses kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so the destroyer would not touch Israel.

translationNotes.term: the servant girl behind the hand mill
translationNotes.note: A saddle quern: a lower stone and an upper stone worked by hand, hours a day, to make the household's flour. It was the lowest job in the house, which is why Exodus 11:5 uses it to mark the bottom of Egyptian society against Pharaoh at the top. Deuteronomy 24:6 forbids taking a millstone as a pledge because it takes a family's food.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּלֵי־כֶסֶף וּכְלֵי זָהָב (kele-khesef u-khele zahav)
translationNotes.note: The word kelim covers vessels, jewelry, and worked metal generally, weighed rather than coined; minted currency did not reach the region until many centuries later. Exodus 3:21-22 announced this, and Exodus 12:35-36 records it happening. The same metal reappears as the tabernacle offering in Exodus 35.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא יֶחֱרַץ־כֶּלֶב לְשֹׁנוֹ (lo yecheratz-kelev leshono), 'no dog shall sharpen its tongue'
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew idiom at 11:7 is a dog sharpening its tongue, meaning to so much as growl. Dogs in that world were scavengers around a settlement, not pets, and a village of them going quiet is a picture of nothing whatever happening. Set against the 'great cry' over Egypt in 11:6, the line measures the distinction God is making between the two peoples.

The hour is announced in advance at 11:4 and reported as kept at 12:29. Night was reckoned in three watches rather than by clock hours (Judges 7:19 names the middle one), so midnight is the join between the first watch and the middle: the deepest point of the night, when a household is asleep and a court is not sitting.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses announces that God will strike down every firstborn in Egypt at midnight, sparing the Israelites; he instructs the people to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold before departing. The Lord will harden Pharaoh's heart so that his refusal multiplies God's wonders.

headings.text: The Plague on the Firstborn Foretold

stories.title: 🩸 Exodus 12
summaryBullets: Now the LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, (12:1).
“This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year. (12:2).
Tell the whole congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month each man must select a lamb for his family, one per household. (12:3).
If the household is too small for a whole lamb, they are to share with the nearest neighbor based on the number of people, and apportion the lamb accordingly. (12:4).
Your lamb must be an unblemished year-old male, and you may take it from the sheep or the goats. (12:5).
You must keep it until the fourteenth day of the month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel will slaughter the animals at twilight. (12:6).
They are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs. (12:7).
They are to eat the meat that night, roasted over the fire, along with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. (12:8).
Do not eat any of the meat raw or cooked in boiling water, but only roasted over the fire— its head and legs and inner parts. (12:9).
Do not leave any of it until morning; before the morning you must burn up any part that is left over. (12:10).
This is how you are to eat it: You must be fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover. (12:11).
On that night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn male, both man and beast, and I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD. (12:12).
The blood on the houses where you are staying will be a sign; when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt. (12:13).
And this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD, as a permanent statute for the generations to come. (12:14).

For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened from the first day through the seventh must be cut off from Israel. (12:15).
On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly, and another on the seventh day. You must not do any work on those days, except to prepare the meals — that is all you may do. (12:16).

So you are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt. You must keep this day as a permanent statute for the generations to come. (12:17).
In the first month you are to eat unleavened bread, from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day. (12:18).

For seven days there must be no leaven found in your houses. If anyone eats something leavened, that person, whether a foreigner or native of the land, must be cut off from the congregation of Israel. (12:19).
You are not to eat anything leavened; eat unleavened bread in all your homes.” (12:20).
Then Moses summoned all the elders of Israel and told them, “Go at once and select for yourselves a lamb for each family, and slaughter the Passover lamb. (12:21).
Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe. None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning. (12:22).

When the LORD passes through to strike down the Egyptians, He will see the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe and will pass over that doorway; so He will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses and strike you down. (12:23).
And you are to keep this command as a permanent statute for you and your descendants. (12:24).
When you enter the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, you are to keep this service. (12:25).
When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’ (12:26).

you are to reply, ‘It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when He struck down the Egyptians and spared our homes.’” Then the people bowed down and worshiped. (12:27).
And the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron. (12:28).

Now at midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn male in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, as well as all the firstborn among the livestock. (12:29).
During the night Pharaoh got up — he and all his officials and all the Egyptians — and there was loud wailing in Egypt; for there was no house without someone dead. (12:30).
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, “Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. (12:31).
Take your flocks and herds as well, just as you have said, and depart! And bless me also.” (12:32).
And in order to send them out of the land quickly, the Egyptians urged the people on. “For otherwise,” they said, “we are all going to die!” (12:33).
So the people took their dough before it was leavened, carrying it on their shoulders in kneading bowls wrapped in clothing. (12:34).
Furthermore, the Israelites acted on Moses’ word and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing. (12:35).
And the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request. In this way they plundered the Egyptians. (12:36).
The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth with about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children. (12:37).
And a mixed multitude also went up with them, along with great droves of livestock, both flocks and herds. (12:38).

Since their dough had no leaven, the people baked what they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened loaves. For when they had been driven out of Egypt, they could not delay and had not prepared any provisions for themselves. (12:39).
Now the duration of the Israelites’ stay in Egypt was 430 years. (12:40).
At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt. (12:41).

Because the LORD kept a vigil that night to bring them out of the land of Egypt, this same night is to be a vigil to the LORD, to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come. (12:42).
And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the statute of the Passover: No foreigner is to eat of it. (12:43).
But any slave who has been purchased may eat of it, after you have circumcised him. (12:44).
A temporary resident or hired hand shall not eat the Passover. (12:45).
It must be eaten inside one house. You are not to take any of the meat outside the house, and you may not break any of the bones. (12:46).
The whole congregation of Israel must celebrate it. (12:47).

If a foreigner resides with you and wants to celebrate the LORD’s Passover, all the males in the household must be circumcised; then he may come near to celebrate it, and he shall be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised man may eat of it. (12:48).
The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner who resides among you.” (12:49).
Then all the Israelites did this — they did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron. (12:50).
And on that very day the LORD brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions. (12:51).
crossRefs: Leviticus 23:5-8: The Passover on the fourteenth of the first month and the seven days of Unleavened Bread that follow.
Numbers 9:1-14: A second Passover appointed for anyone unclean or away on a journey.
Deuteronomy 16:1-8: Passover kept in the month of Abib, at the place the LORD chooses.
1 Corinthians 5:6-8: Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, so keep the feast without the old leaven.
John 19:36: Not one of His bones will be broken, the rule laid down for the Passover lamb.

translationNotes.note: A small, fragrant herb (Origanum syriacum / Syrian oregano), growing in rocky soil. Bunches of hyssop were used to apply Passover blood to the doorposts (Exodus 12:22), in leper-cleansing rituals (Leviticus 14:6), and held up to Jesus on the cross with a wine-soaked sponge (John 19:29).

Abib means the green ear of grain, and Exodus 9:31 uses the same word for barley standing in the ear. So the first month is named for the state of the barley crop, and the calendar in Exodus 12:2 starts in spring, in our March or April. After the exile the month is called Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1; Esther 3:7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּין הָעַרְבַּיִם (bein ha-arbayim), 'between the two evenings'
