translationNotes.note: The window for killing the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day. In the Second Temple period it was reckoned as the afternoon: Josephus writes in The Jewish War 6.423 that the lambs were killed from the ninth hour to the eleventh, roughly three to five in the afternoon.

Sharp-tasting greens eaten with the roasted lamb and the unleavened bread, the same three elements repeated in Numbers 9:11. The root is the same one behind Marah, the bitter water of Exodus 15:23, and behind the bitter lives of Exodus 1:14.

Exodus 12:12 states the purpose plainly: judgment on Egypt's gods, not only on its people. Egyptian religion tied the state's food, weather, health, and kingship to named deities, and Pharaoh himself held divine standing as the son of Ra. Numbers 33:4 repeats the verdict while Egypt is burying its dead.

Non-Israelites who left Egypt with Israel. The Passover statute in Exodus 12:48-49 makes room for them: a foreigner who is circumcised keeps the feast and stands under the same law as a native. Numbers 11:4 shows this group again in the wilderness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׂה (seh), a lamb or kid from the flock
translationNotes.note: The instructions in Exodus 12:3-7 are deliberately public and deliberately domestic. Every household takes a year-old male from the flock on the tenth day, keeps it in the house four days where the neighbors can see it, kills it at twilight on the fourteenth, and smears the blood on the two doorposts and the lintel where the whole street can see that too. In a country that revered livestock and despised herdsmen, doing this at every Israelite door on the same evening was the plainest possible public act.

translationNotes.term: the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne
translationNotes.note: Exodus 11:5 and 12:29 name the range from the crown prince down to the prisoner in the dungeon and the firstborn of the cattle. The eldest son of Pharaoh was not merely an heir; he was the next living god of Egypt, and the succession of the divine kingship ran through him. Israel is called God's firstborn son back at Exodus 4:22-23, with the warning attached to it, so the final plague answers the claim made there.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּסַח (pesach), the noun - פָּסַח (pasach), the verb - Greek: πάσχα (pascha)
translationNotes.note: The verb at 12:13 and 12:23 is pasach, and the text defines the name by the action: the LORD passes over the marked doors and does not let the destroyer in. Isaiah 31:5 uses the same verb of God shielding Jerusalem. Pesach names both the festival and the animal killed for it, so 12:21 says to take a pesach and slaughter it. The Greek pascha, taken straight from the Hebrew, is the word Paul uses at 1 Corinthians 5:7.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַצָּה (matsah), plural מַצּוֹת (matsot) - חָמֵץ (chametz), leavened
translationNotes.note: Matsah is flat bread made without a starter, and 12:39 gives the reason on the night itself: they were driven out and had no time to let dough rise. The seven-day rule at 12:15-20 goes further than the meal; every scrap of chametz is to be out of the house, and anyone eating it is cut off from Israel. That is why searching the house for leaven became a fixed part of the preparation, and why Paul can use leaven as a figure at 1 Corinthians 5:6-8.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה וְאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה (sheloshim shanah ve-arba meot shanah)
translationNotes.note: Verses 12:40-41 give the length of the stay in Egypt as 430 years and say the departure fell on the day the term ended. Genesis 15:13 had told Abraham his offspring would be strangers and afflicted 400 years. Paul counts the same 430 from the promise to the law at Galatians 3:17, and 1 Kings 6:1 sets 480 years between the Exodus and the founding of Solomon's temple.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses on the Passover meal - a lamb to be slaughtered, its blood marked on doorframes, eaten with bitter herbs and unleavened bread - and that night strikes down all Egyptian firstborns while passing over marked Israelite homes; Pharaoh then orders Israel to leave, and they depart Egypt with plundered goods after 430 years.

headings.text: The Tenth Plague: Death of the Firstborn

stories.title: 🌊 Exodus 13
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (13:1).
“Consecrate to Me every firstborn male. The firstborn from every womb among the Israelites belongs to Me, both of man and beast.” (13:2).

So Moses told the people, “Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; for the LORD brought you out of it by the strength of His hand. And nothing leavened shall be eaten. (13:3).
Today, in the month of Abib, you are leaving. (13:4).

And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites — the land He swore to your fathers that He would give you, a land flowing with milk and honey — you shall keep this service in this month. (13:5).
For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD. (13:6).
Unleavened bread shall be eaten during those seven days. Nothing leavened may be found among you, nor shall leaven be found anywhere within your borders. (13:7).
And on that day you are to explain to your son, ‘This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.’ (13:8).
It shall be a sign for you on your hand and a reminder on your forehead that the Law of the LORD is to be on your lips. For with a mighty hand the LORD brought you out of Egypt. (13:9).
Therefore you shall keep this statute at the appointed time year after year. (13:10).
And after the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites and gives it to you, as He swore to you and your fathers, (13:11).
you are to present to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb. All the firstborn males of your livestock belong to the LORD. (13:12).
You must redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb, and if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck. And every firstborn of your sons you must redeem. (13:13).
In the future, when your son asks you, ‘What does this mean?’ you are to tell him, ‘With a mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (13:14).

And when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both of man and beast. This is why I sacrifice to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb, but I redeem all the firstborn of my sons.’ (13:15).
So it shall serve as a sign on your hand and a symbol on your forehead, for with a mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt.” (13:16).

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter. For God said, “If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt.” (13:17).
So God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the Israelites left the land of Egypt arrayed for battle. (13:18).

Moses took the bones of Joseph with him because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath when he said, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from this place.” (13:19).
They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham on the edge of the wilderness. (13:20).
And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night, so that they could travel by day or night. (13:21).
Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people. (13:22).
crossRefs: Numbers 3:11-13: The Levites taken by God in place of every firstborn male of Israel.
Numbers 18:15-16: Every firstborn son redeemed at one month old for five shekels of the sanctuary.
Luke 2:22-24: Joseph and Mary bring the firstborn Jesus to the temple with the offering the law required.
Genesis 50:24-26: Joseph makes the sons of Israel swear to carry his bones up out of Egypt.
Joshua 24:32: Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem in the plot of ground Jacob bought.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַמּוּד עָנָן (ammud anan), pillar of cloud - עַמּוּד אֵשׁ (ammud esh), pillar of fire
translationNotes.note: An ammud is an upright column, the same word used for the posts holding up the tabernacle curtains (26:32). Verses 13:21-22 say neither pillar ever left its place in front of the people, so the column functions as a marching guide that can be seen from anywhere in a camp of that size, by day as a cloud and by night as fire. Numbers 9:15-23 makes the rule explicit: the camp moved when it lifted and stayed when it settled.

To buy back by paying a set price. Every firstborn male belonged to God, so a firstborn son and a firstborn donkey had to be bought back rather than sacrificed; Numbers 18:16 fixes the price for a son at five shekels of the sanctuary, about 57 grams of silver. Luke 2:22-24 shows the rite still being kept.

translationNotes.term: a sign on your hand and a reminder on your forehead
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְאוֹת עַל־יָדְכָה וּלְטוֹטָפֹת בֵּין עֵינֶיךָ (le-ot al-yadkhah u-le-totafot bein einekha)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew totafot appears only in this command and in Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18. It is the line behind the leather boxes of scripture, tefillin, called phylacteries in Matthew 23:5, worn on the arm and the head.

translationNotes.term: the road through the land of the Philistines
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים (derekh erets Pelishtim)
translationNotes.note: The coastal highway from the eastern Delta to Gaza, the shortest way into Canaan at roughly 150 miles, and the route Egypt used for its armies. It was garrisoned with forts and wells at intervals, which is exactly why Exodus 13:17 says God did not lead Israel that way.

Succoth is the first stop out of Egypt (12:37, 13:20) and its name means booths, the temporary branch shelters people threw up when they camped. The Feast of Booths in Leviticus 23:42-43 is named for the same thing and given the same reason: so Israel would remember living in shelters on the way out of Egypt. Etham is described as on the edge of the wilderness, which means the party had reached the point where cultivated Delta land stops.

Joseph made Israel swear to carry his bones out (Genesis 50:25), and 13:19 records Moses collecting on that oath while the country is in chaos behind him. Egyptians embalmed and Genesis 50:26 says Joseph was embalmed and put in a coffin, so there was something to carry. Joshua 24:32 finishes the account: they buried him at Shechem, in the plot of ground Jacob had bought.

stories.keyTakeaway: God commands Moses to consecrate all firstborn males and establish an annual Feast of Unleavened Bread to commemorate the exodus; he then leads Israel away from Egypt by the desert road toward the Red Sea, guiding them by a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, while Moses carries Joseph's bones as promised.

headings.text: The Pillars of Cloud and Fire

stories.title: 🌊 Exodus 14
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (14:1).
“Tell the Israelites to turn back and encamp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. You are to encamp by the sea, directly opposite Baal-zephon. (14:2).
For Pharaoh will say of the Israelites, ‘They are wandering the land in confusion; the wilderness has boxed them in.’ (14:3).

And I will harden Pharaoh’s heart so that he will pursue them. But I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh and all his army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD.” So this is what the Israelites did. (14:4).
When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, Pharaoh and his officials changed their minds about them and said, “What have we done? We have released Israel from serving us.” (14:5).
So Pharaoh prepared his chariot and took his army with him. (14:6).
He took 600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them. (14:7).
And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt so that he pursued the Israelites, who were marching out defiantly. (14:8).
The Egyptians— all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots, horsemen and troops— pursued the Israelites and overtook them as they camped by the sea near Pi-hahiroth, opposite Baal-zephon. (14:9).
As Pharaoh approached, the Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians marching after them, and they were terrified and cried out to the LORD. (14:10).
They said to Moses, “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us into the wilderness to die? What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt? (14:11).
Did we not say to you in Egypt, ‘Leave us alone so that we may serve the Egyptians’? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.” (14:12).

But Moses told the people, “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD’s salvation, which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. (14:13).
The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.” (14:14).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to go forward. (14:15).
And as for you, lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, so that the Israelites can go through the sea on dry ground. (14:16).
And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they will go in after them. Then I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh and all his army and chariots and horsemen. (14:17).
The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I am honored through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.” (14:18).
And the angel of God, who had gone before the camp of Israel, withdrew and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from before them and stood behind them, (14:19).
so that it came between the camps of Egypt and Israel. The cloud was there in the darkness, but it lit up the night. So all night long neither camp went near the other. (14:20).
Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land. So the waters were divided, (14:21).
and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left. (14:22).
And the Egyptians chased after them— all Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, and horsemen— and followed them into the sea. (14:23).
At morning watch, however, the LORD looked down on the army of the Egyptians from the pillar of fire and cloud, and He threw their camp into confusion. (14:24).
He caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving. “Let us flee from the Israelites,” said the Egyptians, “for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” (14:25).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.” (14:26).
So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its normal state. As the Egyptians were retreating, the LORD swept them into the sea. (14:27).
The waters flowed back and covered the chariots and horsemen — the entire army of Pharaoh that had chased the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived. (14:28).
But the Israelites had walked through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left. (14:29).
That day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore. (14:30).
When Israel saw the great power that the LORD had exercised over the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses. (14:31).
crossRefs: Psalm 106:9-12: He rebuked the Red Sea and led them through the depths as through a desert.
Isaiah 63:11-13: The LORD who brought them through the depths, leading them like a horse through open country.
Hebrews 11:29: By faith they passed through the Red Sea as on dry land, and the Egyptians drowned attempting it.
1 Corinthians 10:1-2: All were under the cloud and all passed through the sea, baptized into Moses.
Joshua 4:22-24: The Jordan dried up before Israel just as the LORD had dried up the Red Sea.

translationNotes.note: The same column that led the march is used here as a barrier. At 14:19-20 it moves from the front of the column to the rear and stands between the two armies all night, dark on one side and lit on the other, which stops the Egyptians closing the distance. At 14:24 the LORD looks down at the Egyptian army from it in the morning watch and throws them into confusion.

Literally 'sea of reeds.' Suf is the same word used for the reeds along the Nile where Moses' basket was placed in Exodus 2:3-5. The name also belongs to the Gulf of Aqaba, where 1 Kings 9:26 puts Solomon's port at Ezion-geber, so it covers more water than the English name suggests.

The Egyptian chariot was a light two-wheeled platform pulled by two horses and crewed by two men, a driver and an archer. Speed on firm ground was its whole advantage, which makes the detail in Exodus 14:25 pointed: the wheels bog down and the crews lose the one thing they had.

Israel divided the night into three watches of about four hours; Judges 7:19 names the middle watch, and this is the last one, running to sunrise. Roman practice later used four watches, which is the reckoning behind Mark 13:35.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִגְדֹּל (Migdol), a tower or fort - בַּעַל צְפוֹן (Baal Tsefon), lord of the north
translationNotes.note: Three landmarks fix the camp in Exodus 14:2, and each one says something. Migdol is the ordinary Hebrew and Egyptian word for a watchtower or frontier fort; Egypt kept a chain of them along its eastern border to control who came and went. Baal-zephon carries the name of the Canaanite storm god who was reckoned lord of the sea and of sailors, so a shrine to him stood at this coastal point. Israel is boxed in with the water ahead, a fort behind, and a sea god's shrine on the shore.

The word at 14:7 is shalishim, third men, the ranking officer on a chariot crew. An Egyptian chariot carried a driver and an archer, so the title probably began with a three-man crew and stayed on as a rank. The same word names the officer who attends a king in 2 Kings 7:2 and 9:25, and it is what the Hebrew calls Pharaoh's best chariot officers here.

stories.keyTakeaway: God commands Israel to camp by the sea, hardens Pharaoh's heart so he pursues them, then parts the sea for the Israelites to cross on dry ground while the pursuing Egyptian army is swept back and drowned. Israel witnesses the destruction and trusts in the LORD and Moses.

stories.title: 🌊 Exodus 15
summaryBullets: Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD: “I will sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted. The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea. (15:1).
The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father’s God, and I will exalt Him. (15:2).
The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is His name. (15:3).
Pharaoh’s chariots and army He has cast into the sea; the finest of his officers are drowned in the Red Sea. (15:4).
The depths have covered them; they sank there like a stone. (15:5).
Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power; Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy. (15:6).
You overthrew Your adversaries by Your great majesty. You unleashed Your burning wrath; it consumed them like stubble. (15:7).
At the blast of Your nostrils the waters piled up; like a wall the currents stood firm; the depths congealed in the heart of the sea. (15:8).
The enemy declared, ‘I will pursue, I will overtake. I will divide the spoils; I will gorge myself on them. I will draw my sword; my hand will destroy them.’ (15:9).
But You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters. (15:10).
Who among the gods is like You, O LORD? Who is like You — majestic in holiness, revered with praises, performing wonders? (15:11).
You stretched out Your right hand, and the earth swallowed them up. (15:12).
With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed; with Your strength You will guide them to Your holy dwelling. (15:13).
The nations will hear and tremble; anguish will grip the dwellers of Philistia. (15:14).
Then the chiefs of Edom will be dismayed; trembling will seize the leaders of Moab; those who dwell in Canaan will melt away, (15:15).
and terror and dread will fall on them. By the power of Your arm they will be as still as a stone until Your people pass by, O LORD, until the people You have bought pass by. (15:16).
You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance — the place, O LORD, You have prepared for Your dwelling, the sanctuary, O Lord, Your hands have established. (15:17).
The LORD will reign forever and ever!” (15:18).
For when Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, and horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought the waters of the sea back over them. But the Israelites walked through the sea on dry ground. (15:19).
Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing. (15:20).
And Miriam sang back to them: “Sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.” (15:21).
Then Moses led Israel from the Red Sea, and they went out into the Desert of Shur. For three days they walked in the desert without finding water. (15:22).
And when they came to Marah, they could not drink the water there because it was bitter. (That is why it was named Marah.) (15:23).
So the people grumbled against Moses, saying, “What are we to drink?” (15:24).

And Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log. And when he cast it into the waters, they were sweetened. There the LORD made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them, (15:25).

saying, “If you will listen carefully to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in His eyes, and pay attention to His commands, and keep all His statutes, then I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians. For I am the LORD who heals you.” (15:26).
Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the waters. (15:27).
crossRefs: Revelation 15:3: The victors sing the song of Moses the servant of God and the song of the Lamb.
Psalm 118:14: The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.
Isaiah 12:2: Isaiah takes up the same line, God is my salvation, my strength and my song.
Deuteronomy 32:1-4: The second song of Moses, taught to Israel at the end of his life.
Numbers 33:8-9: The wilderness itinerary lists Marah, then Elim with its twelve springs and seventy palms.

translationNotes.note: A hand-held frame drum, a wooden hoop with a skin stretched over it, not the jingling instrument the English word suggests. It was the standard instrument of women leading a victory song, as in Judges 11:34 and 1 Samuel 18:6.

The place name is the point: Exodus 15:23 says they could not drink the water because it was bitter, marah, so that is what they called it. Naomi uses the same word of herself in Ruth 1:20. The bitter herbs of the Passover in Exodus 12:8 come from this root as well.
The line in Exodus 15:11 that gives Michael his name, mikhael, 'who is like God.' It is a question with a fixed answer, and Israel's song puts it to the gods of the nation that had just drowned.

translationNotes.term: Elim, twelve springs and seventy palms
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵילִם (Elim), from the word for great trees
translationNotes.note: In desert travel the route is decided by the water, and Exodus 15:22-27 is an itinerary of water: three days with none, then Marah where it was too bitter to drink, then Elim with twelve springs and seventy palm trees. Palms grow where the water table is close to the surface, so the trees are the sign that the springs are permanent. Numbers 33:9 repeats the same count of springs and palms when it lists the stages of the journey.

Verse 15:20 is the first time Scripture calls anyone a neviah, and it is Aaron's sister. Others follow: Deborah judges Israel (Judges 4:4), Huldah authenticates the scroll found in the temple (2 Kings 22:14), Isaiah's wife carries the title (Isaiah 8:3), and Anna is in the temple when Jesus is presented (Luke 2:36). Micah 6:4 lists Miriam alongside Moses and Aaron as the three God sent to lead Israel out.

At 15:26, three days after the bitter water at Marah, God attaches a name to Himself out of what has just happened. Several such names are formed the same way in the Torah, each fixed to an event: 'the LORD will provide' at Genesis 22:14 and 'the LORD is my banner' at Exodus 17:15. Rapha covers physical healing and repair generally; 1 Kings 18:30 uses it of Elijah mending a broken altar.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses and the Israelites sing a victory song celebrating God's destruction of Pharaoh's army in the sea; they then travel into the desert, complain about bitter water at Marah, and God makes it drinkable and sets conditions for their continued health.

stories.title: 🌊 Exodus 16
summaryBullets: On the fifteenth day of the second month after they had left the land of Egypt, the whole congregation of Israel set out from Elim and came to the Desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai. (16:1).
And there in the desert the whole congregation of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. (16:2).

“If only we had died by the LORD’s hand in the land of Egypt!” they said. “There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread, but you have brought us into this desert to starve this whole assembly to death!” (16:3).

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions. (16:4).
Then on the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather on the other days.” (16:5).
So Moses and Aaron said to all the Israelites, “This evening you will know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, (16:6).
and in the morning you will see the LORD’s glory, because He has heard your grumbling against Him. For who are we, that you should grumble against us?” (16:7).

And Moses added, “The LORD will give you meat to eat this evening and bread to fill you in the morning, for He has heard your grumbling against Him. Who are we? Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD.” (16:8).
Then Moses said to Aaron, “Tell the whole congregation of Israel, ‘Come before the LORD, for He has heard your grumbling.’” (16:9).
And as Aaron was speaking to the whole congregation of Israel, they looked toward the desert, and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared. (16:10).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (16:11).
“I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Tell them, ‘At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God.’” (16:12).
That evening quail came and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp. (16:13).
When the layer of dew had evaporated, there were thin flakes on the desert floor, as fine as frost on the ground. (16:14).
When the Israelites saw it, they asked one another, “What is it?” For they did not know what it was. So Moses told them, “It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat. (16:15).
This is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Each one is to gather as much as he needs. You may take an omer for each person in your tent.’” (16:16).
So the Israelites did this. Some gathered more, and some less. (16:17).
When they measured it by the omer, he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall. Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat. (16:18).
Then Moses said to them, “No one may keep any of it until morning.” (16:19).
But they did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning, and it became infested with maggots and began to smell. So Moses was angry with them. (16:20).
Every morning each one gathered as much as was needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away. (16:21).
On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much food — two omers per person — and all the leaders of the congregation came and reported this to Moses. (16:22).

He told them, “This is what the LORD has said: ‘Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD. So bake what you want to bake, and boil what you want to boil. Then set aside whatever remains and keep it until morning.’” (16:23).
So they set it aside until morning as Moses had commanded, and it did not smell or contain any maggots. (16:24).
“Eat it today,” Moses said, “because today is a Sabbath to the LORD. Today you will not find anything in the field. (16:25).
For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there.” (16:26).
Yet on the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they did not find anything. (16:27).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and instructions? (16:28).

Understand that the LORD has given you the Sabbath; that is why on the sixth day He will give you bread for two days. On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place.” (16:29).
So the people rested on the seventh day. (16:30).
Now the house of Israel called the bread manna. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey. (16:31).

Moses said, “This is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’” (16:32).
So Moses told Aaron, “Take a jar and fill it with an omer of manna. Then place it before the LORD to be preserved for the generations to come.” (16:33).
And Aaron placed it in front of the Testimony, to be preserved just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (16:34).
The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land where they could settle; they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan. (16:35).
(Now an omer is a tenth of an ephah.) (16:36).
crossRefs: Numbers 11:4-9: Manna described again, along with the craving for meat and the quail that answered it.
Deuteronomy 8:2-3: God humbled Israel with manna to teach that man does not live on bread alone.
Joshua 5:11-12: The manna stops the day after Israel eats the produce of Canaan.
John 6:31-35: Jesus answers the crowd who cite the manna, saying He is the bread of life.
Hebrews 9:4: A gold jar of manna kept inside the ark with Aaron's budded staff and the tablets.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָן (man) - from the question מָן הוּא (man hu), 'what is it?'
translationNotes.note: The name is the people's own question. Verse 16:15 has them asking man hu because they did not know what it was, and 16:31 says Israel called the bread man. The description there is exact: white like coriander seed, tasting of wafers made with honey. It fell six mornings a week for forty years and stopped the day after Israel ate the produce of Canaan (Joshua 5:12), and a jarful was kept in front of the ark as a record (16:33-34; Hebrews 9:4).
A dry-measure unit, about 2 quarts (2 liters). The daily ration of manna in the wilderness was one omer per person (Exodus 16:16); one tenth of an ephah.
The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

The common quail crosses Sinai in enormous numbers on its spring and autumn migration, arriving spent after the sea crossing and easily taken by hand. Exodus 16:13 has them covering the camp in the evening. Numbers 11:31-32 records a second, far larger fall of them.

A wilderness region between Elim and Sinai, named in Exodus 16:1 and Numbers 33:11. It has nothing to do with the English word sin; the Hebrew names for wrongdoing are chet and avon. The similar-looking Wilderness of Zin in Numbers 20:1 is a different place, spelled with a different letter.

Exodus 16:23 is the first time the word Sabbath is used in Scripture as a command, and it arrives four chapters before Sinai, attached to a food ration rather than to a ceremony. Twice as much manna fell on the sixth day, and only that portion kept overnight without spoiling (16:24). Men who went out to gather on the seventh found nothing (16:27).

stories.keyTakeaway: The Israelites grumble about hunger in the desert, and God provides quail at evening and manna each morning, with instructions to gather only what is needed daily and to rest on the seventh day.

stories.title: 🌊 Exodus 17
summaryBullets: Then the whole congregation of Israel left the Desert of Sin, moving from place to place as the LORD commanded. They camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink. (17:1).
So the people contended with Moses, “Give us water to drink.” “Why do you contend with me?” Moses replied. “Why do you test the LORD?” (17:2).
But the people thirsted for water there, and they grumbled against Moses: “Why have you brought us out of Egypt — to make us and our children and livestock die of thirst?” (17:3).
Then Moses cried out to the LORD, “What should I do with these people? A little more and they will stone me!” (17:4).
And the LORD said to Moses, “Walk on ahead of the people and take some of the elders of Israel with you. Take along in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go. (17:5).

Behold, I will stand there before you by the rock at Horeb. And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink.” So Moses did this in the sight of the elders of Israel. (17:6).
He named the place Massah and Meribah because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD, saying, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (17:7).
After this, the Amalekites came and attacked the Israelites at Rephidim. (17:8).
So Moses said to Joshua, “Choose some of our men and go out to fight the Amalekites. Tomorrow I will stand on the hilltop with the staff of God in my hand.” (17:9).
Joshua did as Moses had instructed him and fought against the Amalekites, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. (17:10).
As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. (17:11).

When Moses’ hands grew heavy, they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Then Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on each side, so that his hands remained steady until the sun went down. (17:12).
So Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his army with the sword. (17:13).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Write this on a scroll as a reminder and recite it to Joshua, because I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” (17:14).
And Moses built an altar and named it The LORD Is My Banner. (17:15).
“Indeed,” he said, “a hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD. The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation.” (17:16).
crossRefs: Numbers 20:2-13: Water from the rock a second time at Kadesh, where Moses strikes instead of speaking.
Psalm 95:8-9: Do not harden your hearts as at Meribah, as in the day at Massah in the wilderness.
1 Corinthians 10:4: They drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them.
Deuteronomy 25:17-19: Remember what Amalek did, cutting off the stragglers when you were weary.
1 Samuel 15:1-3: Saul is sent to carry out the sentence pronounced against Amalek here.

translationNotes.note: A matteh is a shepherd's or traveller's rod, and the same word means a tribe, because a tribe is a branch off one stock. This particular staff is the one that turned into a serpent (4:2-4) and struck the Nile (7:20), and 17:5 tells Moses to bring it to the rock in front of the elders so they can see which staff it is. At 17:9 he holds it up over the fight with Amalek.

Both names are made from what happened there, as Exodus 17:7 says outright: they quarrelled and they tested the LORD. Psalm 95:8-9 turns the pair of names into a warning, and Hebrews 3:7-9 quotes that psalm.

A desert people descended from Esau through Eliphaz (Genesis 36:12), so a related nation attacking Israel first. Deuteronomy 25:17-19 adds the detail this chapter leaves out: they cut off the stragglers at the back when Israel was worn out.

translationNotes.term: the Amalekites and what became of them
translationNotes.note: Amalek raided the Negev and the desert margins, and this ambush at Rephidim starts a feud that runs the length of the Old Testament. Balaam calls them first among the nations at Numbers 24:20; they join Midian to strip Israel's harvests in Judges 6:3; Saul loses the kingdom over sparing their king Agag at 1 Samuel 15; David raids them and they burn Ziklag at 1 Samuel 30. Haman, who tries to destroy the whole Jewish people in Esther, is introduced as the Agagite at Esther 3:1.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוָה נִסִּי (YHWH Nissi) - נֵס (nes), a signal pole
translationNotes.note: A nes is not a flag on a stick; it is a pole or standard raised on high ground so that scattered men can see it and rally to it. Isaiah 11:10 and 11:12 use it of a signal raised for the nations. Moses builds an altar after the battle and gives it this name (17:15), which fits what has just happened on the hilltop, with the raised staff visible to the men fighting below.

Named without introduction at 17:10 and 17:12, holding up one of Moses' hands while Aaron holds the other. He turns up twice more: at 24:14 Moses leaves him and Aaron in charge of the camp while he goes up the mountain, and at 31:2 Bezalel, the craftsman who builds the tabernacle, is named as the son of Uri, the son of Hur.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel quarrels with Moses over lack of water at Rephidim, so Moses strikes a rock and water flows out; the Amalekites then attack, and Joshua defeats them while Moses holds up his staff with Aaron and Hur's help.

stories.title: 🌊 Exodus 18
summaryBullets: Now Moses’ father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian, heard about all that God had done for Moses and His people Israel, and how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt. (18:1).
After Moses had sent back his wife Zipporah, his father-in-law Jethro had received her, (18:2).
along with her two sons. One son was named Gershom, for Moses had said, “I have been a foreigner in a foreign land.” (18:3).
The other son was named Eliezer, for Moses had said, “The God of my father was my helper and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.” (18:4).
Moses’ father-in-law Jethro, along with Moses’ wife and sons, came to him in the desert, where he was encamped at the mountain of God. (18:5).
He sent word to Moses, “I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons.” (18:6).
So Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. They greeted each other and went into the tent. (18:7).

Then Moses recounted to his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardships they had encountered along the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. (18:8).
And Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel, whom He had rescued from the hand of the Egyptians. (18:9).
Jethro declared, “Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and of Pharaoh, and who has delivered the people from the hand of the Egyptians. (18:10).
Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods, for He did this when they treated Israel with arrogance.” (18:11).
Then Moses’ father-in-law Jethro brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law in the presence of God. (18:12).
The next day Moses took his seat to judge the people, and they stood around him from morning until evening. (18:13).

When his father-in-law saw all that Moses was doing for the people, he asked, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone as judge, with all the people standing around you from morning till evening?” (18:14).
“Because the people come to me to inquire of God,” Moses replied. (18:15).
“Whenever they have a dispute, it is brought to me to judge between one man and another, and I make known to them the statutes and laws of God.” (18:16).
But Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not good. (18:17).
Surely you and these people with you will wear yourselves out, because the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone. (18:18).
Now listen to me; I will give you some advice, and may God be with you. You must be the people’s representative before God and bring their causes to Him. (18:19).
Teach them the statutes and laws, and show them the way to live and the work they must do. (18:20).

Furthermore, select capable men from among the people — God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain. Appoint them over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. (18:21).

Have these men judge the people at all times. Then they can bring you any major issue, but all minor cases they can judge on their own, so that your load may be lightened as they share it with you. (18:22).
If you follow this advice and God so directs you, then you will be able to endure, and all these people can go home in peace.” (18:23).
Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he said. (18:24).
So Moses chose capable men from all Israel and made them heads over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. (18:25).
And they judged the people at all times; they would bring the difficult cases to Moses, but any minor issue they would judge themselves. (18:26).
Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own land. (18:27).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 1:9-18: Moses recounts appointing commanders and judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
Numbers 11:16-17: Seventy elders receive a share of the Spirit so they can carry the burden with Moses.
Numbers 10:29-32: Moses asks Hobab the Midianite to travel with Israel and be their eyes in the wilderness.
Judges 1:16: The descendants of Moses' father-in-law the Kenite go up with Judah into the desert of Arad.
Acts 6:1-6: The apostles appoint seven men over the daily distribution so the work is shared.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים ... שָׂרֵי מֵאוֹת (sare alafim ... sare meot)
translationNotes.note: A decimal command structure taken straight from military organization and applied to civil justice. Deuteronomy 1:15 repeats it, and 1 Samuel 8:12 shows a king staffing an army the same way. Jethro's advice builds a court of appeal with Moses only at the top.

A specific term for the wife's father, used seven times in this one chapter. Hebrew keeps separate words for each in-law relation where English uses one phrase for all of them. The repetition marks Jethro's standing: a Midianite priest counselling Israel's leader.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּרְשֹׁם (Gershom) - אֱלִיעֶזֶר (Eliezer), 'my God is help'
translationNotes.note: Verses 18:3-4 give both sons and the sentence behind each name. Gershom records that Moses had been a foreigner in a foreign land; Eliezer records that the God of his father delivered him from Pharaoh's sword, which points back to the flight of 2:15. Hebrew names are frequently short statements of this kind, and Scripture usually supplies the sentence when it matters.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֶאֱכָל־לֶחֶם לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (le ekhol-lechem lifne ha-Elohim)
translationNotes.note: At 18:12 Jethro, a Midianite priest, brings a burnt offering and sacrifices, and Aaron and all the elders of Israel come and eat with him in God's presence. A shared meal after a sacrifice was how an agreement was sealed in that world; Genesis 31:54 shows Jacob and Laban doing the same thing after they set up their boundary stone. This is before Sinai and before any Israelite priesthood exists.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jethro visits Moses in the wilderness with his wife and sons, hears of God's deliverance from Egypt, offers sacrifices, and observes Moses judging disputes alone all day. Jethro advises Moses to delegate authority to capable judges over groups of different sizes, keeping only difficult cases for himself; Moses accepts the advice and implements it.

stories.title: ⛰️ Exodus 19
summaryBullets: In the third month, on the same day of the month that the Israelites had left the land of Egypt, they came to the Wilderness of Sinai. (19:1).
After they had set out from Rephidim, they entered the Wilderness of Sinai, and Israel camped there in front of the mountain. (19:2).
Then Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain, “This is what you are to tell the house of Jacob and explain to the sons of Israel: (19:3).
‘You have seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself. (19:4).
Now if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations — for the whole earth is Mine. (19:5).
And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you are to speak to the Israelites.” (19:6).
So Moses went back and summoned the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him. (19:7).
And all the people answered together, “We will do everything that the LORD has spoken.” So Moses brought their words back to the LORD. (19:8).

The LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will come to you in a dense cloud, so that the people will hear when I speak with you, and they will always put their trust in you.” And Moses relayed to the LORD what the people had said. (19:9).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow. They must wash their clothes (19:10).
and be prepared by the third day, for on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. (19:11).

And you are to set up a boundary for the people around the mountain and tell them, ‘Be careful not to go up on the mountain or touch its base. Whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death. (19:12).

No hand shall touch him, but he shall surely be stoned or shot with arrows — whether man or beast, he must not live.’ Only when the ram’s horn sounds a long blast may they approach the mountain.” (19:13).
When Moses came down from the mountain to the people, he consecrated them, and they washed their clothes. (19:14).
“Be prepared for the third day,” he said to the people. “Do not draw near to a woman.” (19:15).

On the third day, when morning came, there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram’s horn went out, so that all the people in the camp trembled. (19:16).
Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet with God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain. (19:17).
Mount Sinai was completely enveloped in smoke, because the LORD had descended on it in fire. And the smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked violently. (19:18).
And as the sound of the ram’s horn grew louder and louder, Moses spoke and God answered him in the thunder. (19:19).
The LORD descended to the top of Mount Sinai and called Moses to the summit. So Moses went up, (19:20).
and the LORD said to him, “Go down and warn the people not to break through to see the LORD, lest many of them perish. (19:21).
Even the priests who approach the LORD must consecrate themselves, or the LORD will break out against them.” (19:22).
But Moses said to the LORD, “The people cannot come up Mount Sinai, for You solemnly warned us, ‘Put a boundary around the mountain and set it apart as holy.’” (19:23).
And the LORD replied, “Go down and bring Aaron with you. But the priests and the people must not break through to come up to the LORD, or He will break out against them.” (19:24).
So Moses went down to the people and spoke to them. (19:25).
crossRefs: 1 Peter 2:9: You are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own possession.
Revelation 1:6: He has made us a kingdom and priests to serve His God and Father.
Hebrews 12:18-21: You have not come to a mountain blazing with fire, darkness, gloom, and trumpet blast.
Deuteronomy 4:10-13: The LORD spoke out of the fire at Horeb and declared His covenant, the Ten Commandments.
Exodus 24:3-8: The people again answer that they will do all the LORD has said, and the covenant is sealed with blood.

translationNotes.note: A berit is a formal, sworn agreement, the instrument used between kings as well as between God and a people. The idiom for making one is to cut a covenant, from the cutting of animals that went with the oath (Genesis 15:9-18; Jeremiah 34:18). Verse 19:5 states the terms of this one plainly, obey My voice and keep My covenant, and the rest of the book is what is being agreed to.

Nesher is usually rendered eagle, but Micah 1:16 describes the bird as bald, which fits the griffon vulture, the great soaring bird of the region with a wingspan approaching nine feet. Deuteronomy 32:11 develops the same picture of the bird stirring its nest and carrying its young.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹבֵל (yovel) in verse 13 - שׁוֹפָר (shofar) in verse 16
translationNotes.note: Two words in the same scene. Yovel is the ram's horn, and it is the word behind 'jubilee': Leviticus 25:9-10 has the yovel sounded on the Day of Atonement to open the fiftieth year. Shofar is the horn as an instrument of signal and alarm.

Said of the whole nation in Exodus 19:6, before Aaron's line is set apart at all. 1 Peter 2:9 and Revelation 1:6 both take the phrase up. It describes Israel's job among the nations, not a rank inside Israel.

translationNotes.term: Mount Sinai, and where it is
translationNotes.note: The mountain carries two names in Scripture, Sinai and Horeb, used of the same place (compare Exodus 19:11 with Exodus 3:1 and Deuteronomy 4:10). Its exact location is not stated. The traditional identification is Jebel Musa in the granite mountains of the southern Sinai peninsula, where Christian hermits settled from the fourth century AD and Justinian later walled in the monastery that still stands there. Other locations have been proposed. What the text does give is the distance and the timing: three months out of Egypt (19:1), and a mountain in wilderness that a whole nation could camp in front of.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַגְבֵּל (hagbel), to set a limit
translationNotes.note: Before anything is spoken, the people wash their clothes, abstain, and a line is drawn around the base that neither man nor animal may cross, on pain of death, and even then no hand may touch the offender; he is shot or stoned from a distance (19:10-13). Exodus 19:21-24 has the warning repeated twice more, and only Moses and Aaron are allowed up. The tabernacle later works on the same graded principle: courtyard, holy place, and an innermost room entered once a year.

A segullah is a king's personal property, the private treasure held apart from the state holdings. The matching word is attested outside Hebrew for exactly that: Akkadian sikiltum and Ugaritic sglt, the latter used of a king in relation to his overlord in a letter from Ras Shamra. Verse 19:5 uses it of Israel and immediately adds 'for the whole earth is Mine,' so the claim is not that God owns nothing else. Deuteronomy 7:6, 14:2 and Malachi 3:17 repeat the word.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel reaches the Desert of Sinai; Moses relays God's covenant offer to make them a kingdom of priests if they obey, and the people agree. After three days of consecration, God descends on Mount Sinai in fire and smoke with thunder and trumpet blasts while Moses receives instructions about boundary restrictions.

stories.title: ⛰️ Exodus 20
summaryBullets: And God spoke all these words: (20:1).
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (20:2).
You shall have no other gods before Me. (20:3).
You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath. (20:4).

You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me, (20:5).
but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments. (20:6).
You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain. (20:7).
Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. (20:8).
Six days you shall labor and do all your work, (20:9).

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work— neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates. (20:10).

For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy. (20:11).
Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. (20:12).
You shall not murder. (20:13).
You shall not commit adultery. (20:14).
You shall not steal. (20:15).
You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. (20:16).
You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.” (20:17).
When all the people witnessed the thunder and lightning, the sounding of the ram’s horn, and the mountain enveloped in smoke, they trembled and stood at a distance. (20:18).
“Speak to us yourself and we will listen,” they said to Moses. “But do not let God speak to us, or we will die.” (20:19).
“Do not be afraid,” Moses replied. “For God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.” (20:20).
And the people stood at a distance as Moses approached the thick darkness where God was. (20:21).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “This is what you are to tell the Israelites: ‘You have seen for yourselves that I have spoken to you from heaven. (20:22).
You are not to make any gods alongside Me; you are not to make for yourselves gods of silver or gold. (20:23).

You are to make for Me an altar of earth, and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and goats and cattle. In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you. (20:24).
Now if you make an altar of stones for Me, you must not build it with stones shaped by tools; for if you use a chisel on it, you will defile it. (20:25).
And you must not go up to My altar on steps, lest your nakedness be exposed on it.’ (20:26).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 5:6-21: The Ten Commandments given again forty years later, with the Sabbath tied to the deliverance from Egypt.

Deuteronomy 24:16: The same law forbids a court to put fathers to death for their children or children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin, which is how Israel was to apply the visiting of iniquity in 20:5.
Ezekiel 18:19-20: God stops Israel quoting the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and states flatly that a son will not bear the iniquity of his father.
Matthew 5:21-28: Jesus takes the commandments against murder and adultery down to anger and the lustful look.
Romans 13:8-10: Paul lists adultery, murder, theft, and coveting from this chapter and sums them all up in 'Love your neighbor as yourself.'

translationNotes.note: The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדְּבָרִים (aseret ha-devarim), 'the ten words' - Greek: δέκα λόγοι (deka logoi)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew calls them ten words, not ten commandments; Exodus 34:28 and Deuteronomy 4:13 use that phrase. The Greek deka logoi gives us Decalogue. Exodus 20 itself never numbers them, which is why traditions divide them differently while keeping the same text.

Shav means empty, worthless, or false. The command covers more than cursing: it forbids attaching God's name to what is empty, above all a false oath, which Leviticus 19:12 spells out as swearing falsely by the name. Matthew 5:33-37 addresses the same abuse.

translationNotes.term: an altar of earth, stones not shaped by tools
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִזְבַּח אֲדָמָה (mizbach adamah) - אַבְנֵי גָזִית (avne gazit), 'cut stones'
translationNotes.note: Exodus 20:24-26 rules out dressed stone and steps. The altar had to be piled earth or unworked field stone, and the priest had to be able to serve without climbing. Joshua 8:30-31 builds exactly this kind of altar on Mount Ebal and cites this command.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָצַח (ratsach), unlawful killing - הָרַג (harag), to kill generally - הֵמִית (hemith), to put to death judicially - נָכָה (nakah), to strike down
translationNotes.note: The command at 20:13 uses ratsach, and 'murder' renders it better than 'kill' because the same body of law commands executions (21:12) and sends Israel to war. Hebrew has other verbs for those: harag is the general word, used of Cain killing Abel (Genesis 4:8) and of the Levites at Exodus 32:27; hemith, the causative of 'to die,' is the courtroom word, used with harag in one breath at Deuteronomy 13:9; nakah means to strike down, as Moses strikes the Egyptian at Exodus 2:12. Four verbs arrive in English as one, which is how a reader ends up thinking the sixth commandment forbids things the next chapter commands.

translationNotes.term: Written with the finger of God
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֻחֹת אֶבֶן (luchot even), tablets of stone - מִכְתַּב אֱלֹהִים (mikhtav Elohim), 'the writing of God'
translationNotes.note: The ten words were not dictated to Moses for him to write down. Exodus 31:18 says the two stone tablets were inscribed with the finger of God, and 32:16 says the tablets were God's work and the writing was God's writing, cut into the stone. Moses breaks that first pair at 32:19. Deuteronomy 10:1-5 has him cut a second pair and place them in the ark.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קוֹלֹת (qolot), thunder, literally 'voices' - לַפִּידִם (lappidim), torches
translationNotes.note: Exodus 20:18 reports what the assembly experienced while the commandments were spoken, and the Hebrew is stranger than the English: the people were seeing the voices and the torches and the sound of the horn and the mountain smoking. Qolot is the ordinary plural of 'voice' and is the standard word for thunder, and lappidim means torches rather than lightning. The people fell back, stood at a distance, and asked Moses to listen for them, which Deuteronomy 5:23-27 records in their own words. Hebrews 12:18-21 looks back on this mountain and quotes Moses saying 'I am terrified and trembling.'

Qanna is used in Scripture only of God, and it is the word for a husband's response to a wife's unfaithfulness (Numbers 5:14 uses the noun for exactly that). It is not envy, which wants what belongs to someone else; it is a claim on what is already one's own. Exodus 34:14 goes further and says His name is Jealous. The clause that follows at 20:5-6 sets the reach: iniquity visited to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Him, covenant love to a thousand generations of those who love Him.

stories.keyTakeaway: God declares ten commandments to the Israelites covering worship, the Sabbath, family, and conduct toward others; the people fear God's presence and ask Moses to speak for them instead, and God instructs them on making altars of earth or unworked stone.

stories.title: ⛰️ Exodus 21
summaryBullets: “These are the ordinances that you are to set before them: (21:1).
If you buy a Hebrew servant, he is to serve you for six years. But in the seventh year, he shall go free without paying anything. (21:2).
If he arrived alone, he is to leave alone; if he arrived with a wife, she is to leave with him. (21:3).
If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, and only the man shall go free. (21:4).
But if the servant declares, ‘I love my master and my wife and children; I do not want to go free,’ (21:5).
then his master is to bring him before the judges. And he shall take him to the door or doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl. Then he shall serve his master for life. (21:6).
And if a man sells his daughter as a servant, she is not to go free as the menservants do. (21:7).

If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master who had designated her for himself, he must allow her to be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, since he has broken faith with her. (21:8).
And if he chooses her for his son, he must deal with her as with a daughter. (21:9).
If he takes another wife, he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of his first wife. (21:10).
If, however, he does not provide her with these three things, she is free to go without monetary payment. (21:11).
Whoever strikes and kills a man must surely be put to death. (21:12).
If, however, he did not lie in wait, but God allowed it to happen, then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee. (21:13).
But if a man schemes and acts willfully against his neighbor to kill him, you must take him away from My altar to be put to death. (21:14).
Whoever strikes his father or mother must surely be put to death. (21:15).
Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession. (21:16).
Anyone who curses his father or mother must surely be put to death. (21:17).
If men are quarreling and one strikes the other with a stone or a fist, and he does not die but is confined to bed, (21:18).

then the one who struck him shall go unpunished, as long as the other can get up and walk around outside with his staff. Nevertheless, he must compensate the man for his lost work and see that he is completely healed. (21:19).
If a man strikes his manservant or maidservant with a rod, and the servant dies by his hand, he shall surely be punished. (21:20).
However, if the servant gets up after a day or two, the owner shall not be punished, since the servant is his property. (21:21).

If men who are fighting strike a pregnant woman and her child is born prematurely, but there is no further injury, he shall surely be fined as the woman’s husband demands and as the court allows. (21:22).
But if a serious injury results, then you must require a life for a life — (21:23).
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, (21:24).
burn for burn, wound for wound, and stripe for stripe. (21:25).
If a man strikes and blinds the eye of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the eye. (21:26).
And if he knocks out the tooth of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the tooth. (21:27).
If an ox gores a man or woman to death, the ox must surely be stoned, and its meat must not be eaten. But the owner of the ox shall not be held responsible. (21:28).
But if the ox has a habit of goring, and its owner has been warned yet does not restrain it, and it kills a man or woman, then the ox must be stoned and its owner must also be put to death. (21:29).
If payment is demanded of him instead, he may redeem his life by paying the full amount demanded of him. (21:30).
If the ox gores a son or a daughter, it shall be done to him according to the same rule. (21:31).
If the ox gores a manservant or maidservant, the owner must pay thirty shekels of silver to the master of that servant, and the ox must be stoned. (21:32).
If a man opens or digs a pit and fails to cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, (21:33).
the owner of the pit shall make restitution; he must pay its owner, and the dead animal will be his. (21:34).
If a man’s ox injures his neighbor’s ox and it dies, they must sell the live one and divide the proceeds; they also must divide the dead animal. (21:35).
But if it was known that the ox had a habit of goring, yet its owner failed to restrain it, he shall pay full compensation, ox for ox, and the dead animal will be his. (21:36).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 19:17-18: Both parties to a dispute stand before the LORD, before the priests and the judges, and the judges investigate thoroughly before sentence is passed; the eye-for-eye standard follows three verses later as what a court hands down.

Leviticus 19:18: The same law forbids seeking revenge or bearing a grudge against any of your own people, which is why the measure-for-measure list at 21:23-25 is not a licence for a wronged man to take it out on his neighbour.
Numbers 35:12: The cities of refuge exist so that a man who kills does not die until he has stood trial before the assembly, the same insistence that a court stands between the parties.

Deuteronomy 23:15-16: A runaway slave must not be handed back to his master but may settle in any town he chooses, the reverse of every surrounding law code and the rule standing over the servant laws in 21:1-11.
Deuteronomy 15:12-18: The seventh-year release repeated, with the master required to send the freed servant off supplied from his flock, his threshing floor, and his winepress.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן (ayin tachat ayin), 'an eye in place of an eye' - בִּפְלִלִים (biflilim), 'as the judges determine'
translationNotes.note: This is a sentencing standard handed to a court, not a licence for private revenge, and it is a ceiling: the penalty may not exceed the injury. Exodus 21:22, four verses earlier, already assesses the payment biflilim, rendered here 'as the court allows.' The same law forbids private payback outright, Leviticus 19:18, 'do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people,' and reserves vengeance to God, Deuteronomy 32:35, 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' which Paul quotes at Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30 quotes again. Every other place the formula appears it sits inside a proceeding: Leviticus 24 holds the man in custody until sentence is given, and Deuteronomy 19 is a courtroom from start to finish, with both parties standing before the priests and the judges (19:17), the judges investigating thoroughly (19:18), and only then life for life, eye for eye (19:21).

translationNotes.term: pierce his ear with an awl
translationNotes.note: A leatherworker's punch. The servant who refuses release is pinned to the doorpost of the house and marked for life as belonging to that household; Deuteronomy 15:16-17 gives the same rite. The mark is visible and permanent, which is the point.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁלֹשִׁים שְׁקָלִים כֶּסֶף (sheloshim sheqalim kesef)
translationNotes.note: The fixed compensation to an owner for a servant killed by someone's ox, about 342 grams of silver. It is the standing value of a slave, which is why the figure carries weight in Zechariah 11:12-13 and again in Matthew 26:15.

translationNotes.term: a place where he may flee
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יָנוּס שָׁמָּה (maqom asher yanus shammah)
translationNotes.note: The first mention of what becomes the cities of refuge. Numbers 35:9-15 and Joshua 20 name six of them, three on each side of the Jordan, for the killer who acted without intent. Exodus 21:14 rules out the same protection for a planned killing, even at the altar.

translationNotes.term: the law codes of the neighbors
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁפָּטִים (mishpatim), judgments or case laws
translationNotes.note: Exodus 21-23 is written as case law, the same form used across the ancient Near East. The best known parallel is the stone stele of Hammurabi of Babylon, carved around 1750 BC, carried off to Susa as loot and dug up there in 1901; it stands in the Louvre and carries 282 rulings. Its laws 250-252 handle the same goring ox that Exodus 21:28-32 handles. The differences are in the text: Hammurabi settles the goring ox entirely in money, while Exodus stones the animal and forbids eating it, and puts the negligent owner's own life in question.

translationNotes.term: the slave who loses an eye or a tooth
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶבֶד (eved), a servant or slave
translationNotes.note: Exodus 21:26-27 frees a slave outright for the loss of an eye or even a single tooth at the owner's hand, with no compensation payable to the owner. Read against 21:20-21, which treats a slave beaten to death as an offense to be punished, the pattern is that injury to the person voids the ownership. Exodus 21:2 also caps Hebrew debt-servitude at six years, and 21:16 makes kidnapping a man to sell him a capital crime, which is the law Joseph's brothers broke in Genesis 37.

translationNotes.term: Six years and then free for nothing
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יֵצֵא לַחׇפְשִׁי חִנָּם (yetse lachophshi chinnam), 'he shall go out free, for nothing'
translationNotes.note: Exodus 21:2 opens the case laws with a term limit on Hebrew servitude: six years, and the seventh brings release at no charge to the servant. The last word, chinnam, means gratis; he buys nothing back and owes nothing. Deuteronomy 15:12-15 restates the rule and adds that he must be sent off loaded from the flock, the threshing floor, and the winepress. This is debt servitude with a clock on it, and the clock runs whether or not the debt is paid.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְגֹנֵב אִישׁ (vegonev ish), 'and one who steals a man'
translationNotes.note: Exodus 21:16 sets death for stealing a man, and it closes both doors: whether the thief has already sold him or still has him in hand. Deuteronomy 24:7 says the same of stealing a fellow Israelite. Because the taking is itself the capital crime, the law bans the trade at its source rather than regulating it, and Genesis 37:26-28 shows the crime being committed when Joseph is sold to a passing caravan for twenty pieces of silver. Paul lists the Greek equivalent, andrapodistes, the slaver, at 1 Timothy 1:10.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוֹר נַגָּח (shor naggach), an ox given to goring
translationNotes.note: Exodus 21:28-32 grades the case by what the owner knew. First offence: the ox is stoned, its meat may not be eaten, and the owner is clear (21:28). If the ox had gored before and the owner was warned and did not pen it, the ox is stoned and the owner's own life is forfeit (21:29), though 21:30 allows a ransom, a kopher, to be laid on him instead. Numbers 35:31 refuses any kopher for a murderer, so negligence can be paid off and murder cannot. If the victim was a slave the owner pays the master thirty shekels and the ox is still stoned (21:32). Prior warning is what turns an accident into the owner's crime.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses presents laws governing Hebrew servants, daughters sold as servants, and capital crimes including murder and assaults on parents; he also establishes rules for injuries, compensation for harm caused by animals, and the principle of proportional justice.

stories.title: ⛰️ Exodus 22
summaryBullets: “If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters or sells it, he must repay five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep. (22:1).
If a thief is caught breaking in and is beaten to death, no one shall be guilty of bloodshed. (22:2).
But if it happens after sunrise, there is guilt for his bloodshed. A thief must make full restitution; if he has nothing, he himself shall be sold for his theft. (22:3).
If what was stolen is actually found alive in his possession— whether ox or donkey or sheep— he must pay back double. (22:4).
If a man grazes his livestock in a field or vineyard and allows them to stray so that they graze in someone else’s field, he must make restitution from the best of his own field or vineyard. (22:5).
If a fire breaks out and spreads to thornbushes so that it consumes stacked or standing grain, or the whole field, the one who started the fire must make full restitution. (22:6).
If a man gives his neighbor money or goods for safekeeping and they are stolen from the neighbor’s house, the thief, if caught, must pay back double. (22:7).
If the thief is not found, the owner of the house must appear before the judges to determine whether he has taken his neighbor’s property. (22:8).

In all cases of illegal possession of an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a garment, or any lost item that someone claims, ‘This is mine,’ both parties shall bring their cases before the judges. The one whom the judges find guilty must pay back double to his neighbor. (22:9).
If a man gives a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any other animal to be cared for by his neighbor, but it dies or is injured or stolen while no one is watching, (22:10).
an oath before the LORD shall be made between the parties to determine whether or not the man has taken his neighbor’s property. The owner must accept the oath and require no restitution. (22:11).
But if the animal was actually stolen from the neighbor, he must make restitution to the owner. (22:12).
If the animal was torn to pieces, he shall bring it as evidence; he need not make restitution for the torn carcass. (22:13).
If a man borrows an animal from his neighbor and it is injured or dies while its owner is not present, he must make full restitution. (22:14).
If the owner was present, no restitution is required. If the animal was rented, the fee covers the loss. (22:15).
If a man seduces a virgin who is not pledged in marriage and sleeps with her, he must pay the full dowry for her to be his wife. (22:16).
If her father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the man still must pay an amount comparable to the bridal price of a virgin. (22:17).
You must not allow a sorceress to live. (22:18).
Whoever lies with an animal must surely be put to death. (22:19).
If anyone sacrifices to any god other than the LORD alone, he must be set apart for destruction. (22:20).
You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt. (22:21).
You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. (22:22).
If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry. (22:23).
My anger will be kindled, and I will kill you with the sword; then your wives will become widows and your children will be fatherless. (22:24).
If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest. (22:25).
If you take your neighbor’s cloak as collateral, return it to him by sunset, (22:26).
because his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in? And if he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am compassionate. (22:27).
You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people. (22:28).
You must not hold back offerings from your granaries or vats. You are to give Me the firstborn of your sons. (22:29).
You shall do likewise with your cattle and your sheep. Let them stay with their mothers for seven days, but on the eighth day you are to give them to Me. (22:30).
You are to be My holy people. You must not eat the meat of a mauled animal found in the field; you are to throw it to the dogs. (22:31).
crossRefs: Leviticus 6:1-5: Property taken by deceit must be restored in full with a fifth added on the day of the guilt offering.
Deuteronomy 24:10-13: Do not keep a poor man's cloak overnight; return it by sunset so he can sleep in it.
Deuteronomy 23:19-20: Do not charge your brother interest on money, food, or anything that can be lent.
Leviticus 19:33-34: The foreigner among you is to be treated as one born among you, and loved as yourself.
James 1:27: Pure religion is to look after orphans and widows in their distress.

translationNotes.note: The outer garment doubled as a blanket, so seizing it overnight left a poor man without bedding; Exodus 22:26-27 orders it returned by sunset. An ostracon from Mesad Hashavyahu near Yavneh-Yam, written in the late seventh century BC, is a field worker's petition complaining that exactly this happened to him.

The word is built on the verb 'to bite.' The law does not regulate a rate; Exodus 22:25 forbids acting as a creditor toward a poor Israelite at all, and Deuteronomy 23:19-20 restates it. The prohibition is about lending inside the covenant community.

To devote something irrevocably to God, so that it can never be redeemed, sold, or put to ordinary use. Leviticus 27:28-29 defines the term, and Joshua 6:17-19 applies it to Jericho. In Exodus 22:20 it is the sentence on anyone who sacrifices to another god.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּתָה (pathah), to entice or persuade; at 22:16 יְפַתֶּה (yephatteh)
translationNotes.note: This verb is the third of three that English versions blur together. Exodus 22:16-17 covers a man who talks an unbetrothed woman into it: he must pay the bride price and marry her, but 22:17 lets her father refuse the marriage outright, and the man pays the silver anyway. Deuteronomy 22:28-29 handles the parallel case with taphas, to take hold of, and Deuteronomy 22:25-27 handles force with chazaq, where the man is executed and the woman is declared guiltless. In Hebrew Bibles these two verses are numbered 22:15-16.

The mohar was paid by the groom to the bride's father, the opposite direction from a dowry, and it is what Exodus 22:16-17 requires whether or not the marriage goes ahead. Shechem offers to pay any mohar Jacob's sons name (Genesis 34:12). Saul asks David for one made of a hundred Philistine foreskins instead of silver, intending David to die collecting it (1 Samuel 18:25). Deuteronomy 22:29 fixes the sum for its case at fifty shekels.

translationNotes.term: The foreigner, the widow, and the orphan
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּר (ger), a resident foreigner - אַלְמָנָה (almanah), widow - יָתוֹם (yatom), orphan
translationNotes.note: These three had no clan to stand up for them, which in a society run on family claims meant no one to press a case at the gate. Exodus 22:21-24 forbids wronging any of them and gives the reason for the first: you were foreigners in Egypt. Then it does something unusual for a law code and names the enforcement, saying that if they cry out He will hear the cry Himself. Deuteronomy 24:17-21 attaches the harvest gleanings to the same three.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְכַשֵּׁפָה (mekhashephah), a woman practicing kishuph
translationNotes.note: The word covers paid ritual work: spells and binding formulas, potions, and figures made to act on a person at a distance.
