Exodus 7:11 uses the masculine form of the same root for the specialists Pharaoh calls in against Moses. Deuteronomy 18:10-11 gives the full list of trades Israel was to have none of, and 2 Kings 9:22 charges Jezebel with these practices by name. Exodus 22:18 puts the practitioner under a death sentence.

stories.keyTakeaway: Laws govern theft and restitution, with penalties ranging from double repayment to death depending on the offense; additional rules address property damage, borrowed animals, seduction, sorcery, idolatry, treatment of foreigners and the poor, lending practices, and offerings to God.

stories.title: ⛰️ Exodus 23
summaryBullets: “You shall not spread a false report. Do not join the wicked by being a malicious witness. (23:1).
You shall not follow the crowd in wrongdoing. When you testify in a lawsuit, do not pervert justice by siding with the crowd. (23:2).
And do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit. (23:3).
If you encounter your enemy’s stray ox or donkey, you must return it to him. (23:4).
If you see the donkey of one who hates you fallen under its load, do not leave it there; you must help him with it. (23:5).
You shall not deny justice to the poor in their lawsuits. (23:6).
Stay far away from a false accusation. Do not kill the innocent or the just, for I will not acquit the guilty. (23:7).
Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous. (23:8).
Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners; for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt. (23:9).
For six years you are to sow your land and gather its produce, (23:10).

but in the seventh year you must let it rest and lie fallow, so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave. Do the same with your vineyard and olive grove. (23:11).

For six days you are to do your work, but on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident. (23:12).
Pay close attention to everything I have said to you. You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips. (23:13).
Three times a year you are to celebrate a feast to Me. (23:14).

You are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread as I commanded you: At the appointed time in the month of Abib you are to eat unleavened bread for seven days, because that was the month you came out of Egypt. No one may appear before Me empty-handed. (23:15).

You are also to keep the Feast of Harvest with the firstfruits of the produce from what you sow in the field. And keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather your produce from the field. (23:16).
Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Lord GOD. (23:17).
You must not offer the blood of My sacrifices with anything leavened, nor may the fat of My feast remain until morning. (23:18).
Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk. (23:19).
Behold, I am sending an angel before you to protect you along the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared. (23:20).
Pay attention to him and listen to his voice; do not defy him, for he will not forgive rebellion, since My Name is in him. (23:21).
But if you will listen carefully to his voice and do everything I say, I will be an enemy to your enemies and a foe to your foes. (23:22).
For My angel will go before you and bring you into the land of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, and Jebusites, and I will annihilate them. (23:23).
You must not bow down to their gods or serve them or follow their practices. Instead, you are to demolish them and smash their sacred stones to pieces. (23:24).
So you shall serve the LORD your God, and He will bless your bread and your water. And I will take away sickness from among you. (23:25).
No woman in your land will miscarry or be barren; I will fulfill the number of your days. (23:26).
I will send My terror ahead of you and throw into confusion every nation you encounter. I will make all your enemies turn and run. (23:27).
I will send the hornet before you to drive the Hivites and Canaanites and Hittites out of your way. (23:28).
I will not drive them out before you in a single year; otherwise the land would become desolate and wild animals would multiply against you. (23:29).
Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you, until you become fruitful and possess the land. (23:30).

And I will establish your borders from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the Euphrates. For I will deliver the inhabitants into your hand, and you will drive them out before you. (23:31).
You shall make no covenant with them or with their gods. (23:32).
They must not remain in your land, lest they cause you to sin against Me. For if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you.” (23:33).
crossRefs: Leviticus 25:1-7: The sabbath year set out in full, with the land resting and its growth left for all to eat.
Leviticus 23:4-44: The full calendar of appointed feasts, month by month.
Deuteronomy 16:16-17: Three times a year every male appears before the LORD, and no one empty-handed.
Deuteronomy 14:21: The same rule against boiling a young goat in its mother's milk.
Joshua 5:13-15: The commander of the LORD's army stands before Joshua with his sword drawn.

translationNotes.note: Verse 23:32 forbids cutting a berit with the peoples of the land or with their gods, and the reason is given in 23:33: a treaty brings their worship in with it. Treaties in that world were sworn in the names of the gods of both parties, and the gods were listed as the witnesses who would enforce the terms, so there was no such thing as a purely political alliance. Joshua 9 shows Israel making one anyway with the Gibeonites, without asking, and being bound by it.

The seventh-day command appears here at 23:12 in its labour form, and the reason given is different from the one at 20:11. Here it is so that the ox and the donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant and the resident foreigner may be refreshed. The people named are the ones with no power to stop working on their own account, and Deuteronomy 5:14-15 makes the same argument from Israel's own slavery in Egypt.

The first portion of each harvest offered to God before the rest could be eaten (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:9-14). Paul calls the resurrected Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20); the guarantee that the full resurrection harvest will follow.

The sabbath year, introduced here and set out fully in Leviticus 25:1-7. The field is not worked and whatever grows on its own is left for the poor and for wild animals. 2 Chronicles 36:20-21 counts the exile as the land finally taking the sabbaths it was owed.

Unleavened Bread in Abib, Harvest at the wheat firstfruits, and Ingathering at the end of the agricultural year. The Hebrew name means the festivals you walk to. Leviticus 23 gives them their fuller names and dates; Deuteronomy 16:16 repeats the requirement to appear.

Named again in Deuteronomy 7:20 and Joshua 24:12 as what God sends ahead of Israel to drive out the inhabitants. Exodus 23:29-30 sets the pace: not in a single year, but little by little, so the land does not go wild.

translationNotes.term: a young goat in its mother's milk
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ (gedi bachalev immo)
translationNotes.note: The command appears three times in the Torah: here, in Exodus 34:26, and in Deuteronomy 14:21. Its threefold repetition is the basis of the later Jewish practice of keeping meat and dairy separate.

translationNotes.term: the Angel in whom My Name is
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְאָךְ (malakh), a messenger - שְׁמִי בְּקִרְבּוֹ (shemi beqirbo), 'My name is in him'
translationNotes.note: Malakh means a messenger, human or otherwise; the same word is used of the men Jacob sends to Esau in Genesis 32:3. Verses 23:20-21 send one ahead of Israel and give an unusual warning with him: do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, because My name is in him. Judges 2:1-3 has this messenger speak in the first person as the one who brought Israel up from Egypt.

stories.keyTakeaway: God gives Israel laws about justice, honesty, rest, and treatment of foreigners; he also promises to send an angel to guide them into Canaan, drive out the inhabitants gradually, and establish their borders from the Red Sea to the Euphrates if they obey and avoid the gods of the land.

stories.title: ⛰️ Exodus 24
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Come up to the LORD — you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel’s elders — and you are to worship at a distance. (24:1).
Moses alone shall approach the LORD, but the others must not come near. And the people may not go up with him.” (24:2).
When Moses came and told the people all the words and ordinances of the LORD, they all responded with one voice: “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” (24:3).
And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. Early the next morning he got up and built an altar at the base of the mountain, along with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. (24:4).
Then he sent out some young men of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD. (24:5).
Moses took half of the blood and put it in bowls, and the other half he splattered on the altar. (24:6).
Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it to the people, who replied, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” (24:7).
So Moses took the blood, splattered it on the people, and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” (24:8).
Then Moses went up with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, (24:9).
and they saw the God of Israel. Under His feet was a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself. (24:10).
But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank. (24:11).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Come up to Me on the mountain and stay here, so that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” (24:12).
So Moses set out with Joshua his attendant and went up on the mountain of God. (24:13).
And he said to the elders, “Wait here for us until we return to you. Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.” (24:14).
When Moses went up on the mountain, the cloud covered it, (24:15).
and the glory of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai. For six days the cloud covered it, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud. (24:16).
And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites. (24:17).
Moses entered the cloud as he went up on the mountain, and he remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. (24:18).
crossRefs: Hebrews 9:18-21: The first covenant was not inaugurated without blood; Moses sprinkled the scroll and the people.
Matthew 26:27-28: This is My blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
Exodus 34:28: Moses is again on the mountain forty days and forty nights without bread or water.
1 Kings 19:8: Elijah travels forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God.
Revelation 4:6: Before the throne is what looks like a sea of glass, clear as crystal.

translationNotes.note: At 24:6-8 Moses puts half the blood of the offerings in basins and throws half against the altar, reads the written terms aloud, and then throws the basin blood over the people with the words 'this is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you.' Both parties are marked with the same blood. Jesus uses that sentence over the cup at Matthew 26:28 and Mark 14:24, and Hebrews 9:19-20 quotes this scene directly.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּבוֹד (kavod), from a root meaning heavy
translationNotes.note: Kavod carries weight before it carries brightness; the same root gives the words for a heavy load and for a liver, the heaviest organ. To have kavod is to have substance that others must reckon with. At 24:16-17 it settles on Sinai as a cloud for six days and looks to the watching Israelites like a fire eating the mountaintop. The same presence fills the finished tabernacle at 40:34-35 and Solomon's temple at 1 Kings 8:10-11.

In the ancient Near East the prized deep blue stone was lapis lazuli, mined in Badakhshan in what is now Afghanistan and traded across the whole region. The hard corundum called sapphire today was not being cut there. Ezekiel 1:26 uses the same stone for the throne he sees.

The written text Moses had made in Exodus 24:4 and read aloud in 24:7, covering the laws of chapters 20 through 23. 2 Kings 23:2 uses the same phrase for the scroll Josiah reads to the nation. Hebrews 9:19 remembers Moses sprinkling blood on this scroll as well as on the people.

translationNotes.term: they saw God, and ate and drank
translationNotes.note: Verses 24:9-11 take Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders part way up the mountain, where they see God, and eat and drink, and the text notes that He did not raise His hand against them. What is described is the pavement under His feet, like sapphire and like the sky itself, not a face; Exodus 33:20 rules that out. Sharing a meal is how a covenant was closed, which is what the seventy have just come up to do.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַעֲרֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (naare bene Yisrael)
translationNotes.note: At 24:5 the burnt offerings and the peace offerings are made by young men of Israel, not by priests. Aaron's line is not set apart until Exodus 28-29, so at this point there is no ordained priesthood to call on; the head of a household still offers for his own people, as Job does for his children in Job 1:5. The order in the book matters here: the covenant is cut first, then the priesthood is established to maintain it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses presents God's laws to the people, who pledge obedience; he performs a covenant ceremony with sacrifices and blood, then ascends the mountain with Aaron and the elders where they see God. Moses continues alone into the cloud for forty days to receive the stone tablets.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 25
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (25:1).
“Tell the Israelites to bring Me an offering. You are to receive My offering from every man whose heart compels him. (25:2).
This is the offering you are to accept from them: gold, silver, and bronze; (25:3).
blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair; (25:4).
ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood; (25:5).
olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense; (25:6).
and onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece. (25:7).
And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them. (25:8).
You must make the tabernacle and design all its furnishings according to the pattern I show you. (25:9).
And they are to construct an ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. (25:10).
Overlay it with pure gold both inside and out, and make a gold molding around it. (25:11).
Cast four gold rings for it and fasten them to its four feet, two rings on one side and two on the other. (25:12).
And make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. (25:13).
Insert the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark, in order to carry it. (25:14).
The poles are to remain in the rings of the ark; they must not be removed. (25:15).
And place inside the ark the Testimony, which I will give you. (25:16).
And you are to construct a mercy seat of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. (25:17).
Make two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat, (25:18).
one cherub on one end and one on the other, all made from one piece of gold. (25:19).
And the cherubim are to have wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat. The cherubim are to face each other, looking toward the mercy seat. (25:20).
Set the mercy seat atop the ark and put the Testimony that I will give you into the ark. (25:21).

And I will meet with you there above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are over the ark of the Testimony; I will speak with you about all that I command you regarding the Israelites. (25:22).
You are also to make a table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. (25:23).
Overlay it with pure gold and make a gold molding around it. (25:24).
And make a rim around it a handbreadth wide and put a gold molding on the rim. (25:25).
Make four gold rings for the table and fasten them to the four corners at its four legs. (25:26).
The rings are to be close to the rim, to serve as holders for the poles used to carry the table. (25:27).
Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold, so that the table may be carried with them. (25:28).
You are also to make the plates and dishes, as well as the pitchers and bowls for pouring drink offerings. Make them out of pure gold. (25:29).
And place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me at all times. (25:30).
Then you are to make a lampstand of pure, hammered gold. It shall be made of one piece, including its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals. (25:31).
Six branches are to extend from the sides of the lampstand — three on one side and three on the other. (25:32).

There are to be three cups shaped like almond blossoms on the first branch, each with buds and petals, three on the next branch, and the same for all six branches that extend from the lampstand. (25:33).
And on the lampstand there shall be four cups shaped like almond blossoms with buds and petals. (25:34).
For the six branches that extend from the lampstand, a bud must be under the first pair of branches, a bud under the second pair, and a bud under the third pair. (25:35).
The buds and branches are to be all of one piece with the lampstand, hammered out of pure gold. (25:36).
Make seven lamps and set them up on the lampstand so that they illuminate the area in front of it. (25:37).
The wick trimmers and their trays must be of pure gold. (25:38).
The lampstand and all these utensils shall be made from a talent of pure gold. (25:39).
See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain. (25:40).
crossRefs: Hebrews 9:1-5: The same furnishings listed again: the lampstand, the table, the ark, and the mercy seat with the cherubim.
Hebrews 8:5: Moses is warned to make everything according to the pattern shown him on the mountain.
1 Chronicles 28:11-19: David hands Solomon a written plan for the temple, put in writing by the LORD's hand.
Leviticus 24:5-9: The twelve loaves of the Bread of the Presence, replaced before the LORD every Sabbath.
Zechariah 4:1-6: A vision of a solid gold lampstand with seven lamps and a bowl of oil above it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרוֹן הָעֵדֻת (aron ha edut), 'chest of the Testimony'
translationNotes.note: An aron is an ordinary chest or box; the same word is used of Joseph's coffin at Genesis 50:26. This one is small, two and a half cubits by one and a half by one and a half, roughly 45 by 27 by 27 inches, made of acacia overlaid with gold inside and out, with rings and poles so it is never handled directly (25:10-15). What went inside it is named at 25:16, the Testimony, meaning the covenant tablets; Hebrews 9:4 adds the jar of manna and Aaron's staff.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

The distance from elbow to fingertip; about 18 inches (45 cm). The standard biblical measure for buildings (Noah's ark, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple) and bodies. Goliath was 'six cubits and a span' tall, about 9 feet 9 in. A 'long cubit' (Ezekiel 40:5) added a handbreadth.
The width of four fingers, about 3 inches (7.5 cm). Used for small dimensions on temple furniture and as a metaphor for the brevity of life (Psalm 39:5).

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

Acacia is the only timber tree of any size in the Sinai, growing in dry wadis where nothing else stands. The wood is hard, dense, and resists insects, which is why every frame, pole, and box of the tabernacle is made from it. The tree gave its name to a camp site as well, Abel-shittim in Numbers 33:49.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּכֵלֶת (tekhelet) - אַרְגָּמָן (argaman) - תּוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי (tolaat shani)
translationNotes.note: The blue and the purple were dyed with fluid from murex sea snails harvested on the Phoenician coast, and each snail yields only a trace, which is why purple cloth marked kings (Judges 8:26; Daniel 5:7; Mark 15:17). The scarlet is literally 'worm of scarlet,' made from the dried bodies of the kermes insect that lives on oak.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁשׁ מָשְׁזָר (shesh moshzar), 'fine twisted linen'
translationNotes.note: Shesh is a loanword from Egyptian for the finest white linen, the fabric Egypt was famous for and in which Joseph was dressed in Genesis 41:42. 'Twisted' means each thread was plied from several strands before weaving, giving a stronger, smoother cloth.

The solid gold lid of the ark, named from the root kaphar, to cover or to make atonement. It is not a chair and nobody sits on it; Exodus 25:22 calls it the place where God meets Moses. The Greek Old Testament renders it hilastērion, the word used in Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 9:5.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים (lechem ha-panim), 'bread of the face'
translationNotes.note: Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out on the gold table and replaced every Sabbath, then eaten by the priests (Leviticus 24:5-9). David ate this bread at Nob when he was on the run (1 Samuel 21:6), and Jesus cites the incident in Matthew 12:3-4.

Seven lamps on a single stand, hammered from one piece of pure gold weighing a talent, about 75 pounds or 34 kilograms. Its cups are shaped like almond blossoms; the almond is the first tree in the land to flower, which is the wordplay Jeremiah 1:11-12 turns on. Zechariah 4:2 sees one in a vision.

translationNotes.term: a tent shrine, and what is not in it
translationNotes.note: The layout would have looked familiar to anyone who had lived in Egypt: an outer court, an inner room, and a small innermost chamber that almost nobody enters, with the holiness rising as you go in. Even the furniture matches the technique, since gilded wooden chests and portable shrines fitted with carrying poles were standard Egyptian temple and tomb equipment, and examples were recovered from Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922. The difference is what stands in the innermost room. An Egyptian sanctuary held the statue of the god. This one holds a box with the covenant tablets inside it (25:16), and above the lid, empty space between two cherubim, where God says He will meet with Moses (25:22).

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses to collect offerings from willing Israelites - gold, silver, bronze, yarn, leather, wood, oil, spices, and gems - to build a sanctuary where he will dwell. God specifies detailed designs for the ark of the covenant with its atonement cover and cherubim, a table for bread, and a seven-lamp gold lampstand, all to be made according to the pattern he will show.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 26
summaryBullets: “You are to construct the tabernacle itself with ten curtains of finely spun linen, each with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and cherubim skillfully worked into them. (26:1).
Each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide — all curtains the same size. (26:2).
Five of the curtains are to be joined together, and the other five joined as well. (26:3).
Make loops of blue material on the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and do the same for the end curtain in the second set. (26:4).
Make fifty loops on one curtain and fifty loops on the end curtain of the second set, so that the loops line up opposite one another. (26:5).
Make fifty gold clasps as well, and join the curtains together with the clasps, so that the tabernacle will be a unit. (26:6).
You are to make curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle — eleven curtains in all. (26:7).
Each of the eleven curtains is to be the same size — thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. (26:8).
Join five of the curtains into one set and the other six into another. Then fold the sixth curtain over double at the front of the tent. (26:9).
Make fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and fifty loops along the edge of the corresponding curtain in the second set. (26:10).
Make fifty bronze clasps and put them through the loops to join the tent together as a unit. (26:11).
As for the overlap that remains of the tent curtains, the half curtain that is left over shall hang down over the back of the tabernacle. (26:12).
And the tent curtains will be a cubit longer on either side, and the excess will hang over the sides of the tabernacle to cover it. (26:13).
Also make a covering for the tent out of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather. (26:14).
You are to construct upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle. (26:15).
Each frame is to be ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. (26:16).
Two tenons must be connected to each other for each frame. Make all the frames of the tabernacle in this way. (26:17).
Construct twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle, (26:18).
with forty silver bases under the twenty frames — two bases for each frame, one under each tenon. (26:19).
For the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, make twenty frames (26:20).
and forty silver bases — two bases under each frame. (26:21).
Make six frames for the rear of the tabernacle, the west side, (26:22).
and two frames for the two back corners of the tabernacle, (26:23).
coupled together from bottom to top and fitted into a single ring. These will serve as the two corners. (26:24).
So there are to be eight frames and sixteen silver bases — two under each frame. (26:25).
You are also to make five crossbars of acacia wood for the frames on one side of the tabernacle, (26:26).
five for those on the other side, and five for those on the rear side of the tabernacle, to the west. (26:27).
The central crossbar in the middle of the frames shall extend from one end to the other. (26:28).
Overlay the frames with gold and make gold rings to hold the crossbars. Also overlay the crossbars with gold. (26:29).
So you are to set up the tabernacle according to the pattern shown you on the mountain. (26:30).
Make a veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it. (26:31).
Hang it with gold hooks on four posts of acacia wood, overlaid with gold and standing on four silver bases. (26:32).
And hang the veil from the clasps and place the ark of the Testimony behind the veil. So the veil will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. (26:33).
Put the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony in the Most Holy Place. (26:34).
And place the table outside the veil on the north side of the tabernacle, and put the lampstand opposite the table, on the south side. (26:35).
For the entrance to the tent, you are to make a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. (26:36).
Make five posts of acacia wood for the curtain, overlay them with gold, use hooks of gold, and cast five bronze bases for them. (26:37).
crossRefs: Exodus 36:8-38: The same curtains, frames, bases, and veil actually made by Bezalel's workmen.
Hebrews 9:2-3: A first room called the Holy Place and, behind the second curtain, the Most Holy Place.
Matthew 27:51: The veil of the temple is torn in two from top to bottom at the death of Jesus.
Numbers 4:24-33: The Gershonites and Merarites assigned to carry the curtains, frames, crossbars, and bases.
2 Chronicles 3:14: Solomon makes a veil of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, with cherubim worked into it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan), a dwelling place, from שָׁכַן (shakan), to settle down
translationNotes.note: Mishkan is built on the verb for settling in and staying, and it names the structure this chapter builds: ten linen curtains over forty-eight upright acacia frames, covered with goat hair, then rams' skins, then a weatherproof outer layer (26:1-14). The Greek Old Testament renders it skene, a tent, which is the word John 1:14 uses when it says the Word became flesh and pitched His tent among us.

The distance from elbow to fingertip; about 18 inches (45 cm). The standard biblical measure for buildings (Noah's ark, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple) and bodies. Goliath was 'six cubits and a span' tall, about 9 feet 9 in. A 'long cubit' (Ezekiel 40:5) added a handbreadth.

Adding up the frames of Exodus 26:15-25 gives a structure about 30 cubits long, 10 wide, and 10 high, that is roughly 45 by 15 feet and 15 feet tall. It is smaller than many houses. The point of the design is portability: every part comes apart and travels on shoulders or carts.

The inner curtain dividing the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, hung on four gold-plated posts. Only the high priest passed it, once a year (Leviticus 16:2). Matthew 27:51 records it torn in two from top to bottom.

The outermost covering of the tent. English versions render tachash as badger skin, porpoise hide, or fine leather, because the Hebrew term is not defined anywhere in Scripture. What is known is that it was durable and weatherproof, and that Ezekiel 16:10 uses the same material for sandals.

Black goat hair is what Bedouin tents are still woven from. The fibre swells when wet and closes the weave, so the cloth sheds rain and stays cool in heat. Exodus 26:7 makes eleven such curtains as the tent over the tabernacle proper.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs how to construct the tabernacle's fabric layers - ten linen curtains joined with gold clasps, eleven goat hair curtains fastened with bronze clasps, and coverings of dyed ram skins - along with acacia wood frames, silver bases, gold-overlaid crossbars, and interior curtains to separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.

headings.text: The Ten Curtains for the Tabernacle
The Eleven Curtains of Goat Hair

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 27
summaryBullets: “You are to build an altar of acacia wood. The altar must be square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high. (27:1).
Make a horn on each of its four corners, so that the horns are of one piece, and overlay it with bronze. (27:2).
Make all its utensils of bronze — its pots for removing ashes, its shovels, its sprinkling bowls, its meat forks, and its firepans. (27:3).
Construct for it a grate of bronze mesh, and make a bronze ring at each of the four corners of the mesh. (27:4).
Set the grate beneath the ledge of the altar, so that the mesh comes halfway up the altar. (27:5).
Additionally, make poles of acacia wood for the altar and overlay them with bronze. (27:6).
The poles are to be inserted into the rings so that the poles are on two sides of the altar when it is carried. (27:7).
Construct the altar with boards so that it is hollow. It is to be made just as you were shown on the mountain. (27:8).
You are also to make a courtyard for the tabernacle. On the south side of the courtyard make curtains of finely spun linen, a hundred cubits long on one side, (27:9).
with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and silver hooks and bands on the posts. (27:10).
Likewise there are to be curtains on the north side, a hundred cubits long, with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and with silver hooks and bands on the posts. (27:11).
The curtains on the west side of the courtyard shall be fifty cubits wide, with ten posts and ten bases. (27:12).
The east side of the courtyard, toward the sunrise, is to be fifty cubits wide. (27:13).
Make the curtains on one side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases, (27:14).
and the curtains on the other side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases. (27:15).
The gate of the courtyard shall be twenty cubits long, with a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. It shall have four posts and four bases. (27:16).
All the posts around the courtyard shall have silver bands, silver hooks, and bronze bases. (27:17).
The entire courtyard shall be a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, with curtains of finely spun linen five cubits high, and with bronze bases. (27:18).
All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, including all its tent pegs and the tent pegs of the courtyard, shall be made of bronze. (27:19).
And you are to command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually. (27:20).

In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil that is in front of the Testimony, Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come. (27:21).
crossRefs: Exodus 38:1-20: The bronze altar and the courtyard built to exactly these measurements.
Leviticus 6:8-13: The fire on the altar is to be kept burning continually and must never go out.
1 Kings 1:50-53: Adonijah takes hold of the horns of the altar and asks Solomon to spare his life.
Leviticus 24:1-4: Pure oil of pressed olives brought so the lamps burn from evening until morning.
1 Samuel 3:3: The lamp of God had not yet gone out when the LORD called Samuel in the night.

translationNotes.note: Four projections worked out of the same piece as the altar's corners. Blood from the sin offering was put on them (Leviticus 4:7), and a man in danger of his life grabbed hold of them for asylum (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28). Four-horned stone altars of this shape have been excavated in Israel, including at Tel Beersheba.

One hundred cubits by fifty, roughly 150 by 75 feet, screened by linen curtains five cubits high, about seven and a half feet. That is taller than a man, so the enclosure was private from the outside. It held about 11,000 square feet, one gate, on the east.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁמֶן זַיִת זָךְ כָּתִית (shemen zayit zakh katit)
translationNotes.note: Katit means beaten. The first oil from olives crushed by hand, before any heat or heavy pressing, burns clean with almost no smoke. Only this grade was allowed for the lamps in the Holy Place (Leviticus 24:2).

Every fitting in the outer courtyard is bronze while everything inside the tent is gold or silver, and the metals mark the zones. Bronze is copper alloyed with tin, harder than either and able to take the heat of a fire; the altar of 27:1-8 is a wooden frame sheathed in it with a grating inside to hold the burning wood. The whole bronze inventory is weighed out at 38:29, seventy talents and 2,400 shekels, roughly 2,400 kilograms.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵר תָּמִיד (ner tamid), a continual lamp
translationNotes.note: Verses 27:20-21 make tending the lamps a standing duty: Aaron and his sons keep them burning from evening until morning, before the LORD, as a permanent statute. Tamid means continual or regular rather than never extinguished, and the lamps are described as set up at twilight and tended each morning (30:7-8). 1 Samuel 3:3 dates a scene by them, before the lamp of God had gone out.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses to build a bronze altar of acacia wood for the tabernacle courtyard, along with detailed specifications for the courtyard enclosure, its posts, curtains, and entrance. Aaron and his sons are to maintain burning lamps in the tent of meeting each evening and morning as a lasting ordinance.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 28
summaryBullets: “Next, have your brother Aaron brought to you from among the Israelites, along with his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, to serve Me as priests. (28:1).
Make holy garments for your brother Aaron, to give him glory and splendor. (28:2).
You are to instruct all the skilled craftsmen, whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom, to make garments for Aaron’s consecration, so that he may serve Me as priest. (28:3).

These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash. They are to make these holy garments for your brother Aaron and his sons, so that they may serve Me as priests. (28:4).
They shall use gold, along with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen. (28:5).
They are to make the ephod of finely spun linen embroidered with gold, and with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn. (28:6).
It shall have two shoulder pieces attached at two of its corners, so it can be fastened. (28:7).
And the skillfully woven waistband of the ephod must be of one piece, of the same workmanship — with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen. (28:8).
Take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel: (28:9).
six of their names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, in the order of their birth. (28:10).
Engrave the names of the sons of Israel on the two stones the way a gem cutter engraves a seal. Then mount the stones in gold filigree settings. (28:11).
Fasten both stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel. Aaron is to bear their names on his two shoulders as a memorial before the LORD. (28:12).
Fashion gold filigree settings (28:13).
and two chains of pure gold, made of braided cord work; and attach these chains to the settings. (28:14).
You are also to make a breastpiece of judgment with the same workmanship as the ephod. Construct it with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen. (28:15).
It must be square when folded over double, a span long and a span wide. (28:16).
And mount on it a setting of gemstones, four rows of stones: In the first row there shall be a ruby, a topaz, and an emerald; (28:17).
in the second row a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond; (28:18).
in the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst; (28:19).
and in the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. Mount these stones in gold filigree settings. (28:20).
The twelve stones are to correspond to the names of the sons of Israel, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes. (28:21).
For the breastpiece, make braided chains like cords of pure gold. (28:22).
You are also to make two gold rings and fasten them to the two corners of the breastpiece. (28:23).
Then fasten the two gold chains to the two gold rings at the corners of the breastpiece, (28:24).
and fasten the other ends of the two chains to the two filigree settings, attaching them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front. (28:25).
Make two more gold rings and attach them to the other two corners of the breastpiece, on the inside edge next to the ephod. (28:26).
Make two additional gold rings and attach them to the bottom of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, on its front, near its seam just above its woven waistband. (28:27).

The rings of the breastpiece shall be tied to the rings of the ephod with a cord of blue yarn, so that the breastpiece is above the waistband of the ephod and does not swing out from the ephod. (28:28).
Whenever Aaron enters the Holy Place, he shall bear the names of the sons of Israel over his heart on the breastpiece of judgment, as a continual reminder before the LORD. (28:29).

And place the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece of judgment, so that they will also be over Aaron’s heart whenever he comes before the LORD. Aaron will continually carry the judgment of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD. (28:30).
You are to make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth, (28:31).
with an opening at its top in the center. Around the opening shall be a woven collar with an opening like that of a garment, so that it will not tear. (28:32).
Make pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn all the way around the lower hem, with gold bells between them, (28:33).
alternating the gold bells and pomegranates around the lower hem of the robe. (28:34).
Aaron must wear the robe whenever he ministers, and its sound will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary before the LORD, so that he will not die. (28:35).
You are to make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it as on a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD. (28:36).
Fasten to it a blue cord to mount it on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban. (28:37).

And it will be worn on Aaron’s forehead, so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things that the sons of Israel consecrate with regard to all their holy gifts. It shall always be on his forehead, so that they may be acceptable before the LORD. (28:38).
You are to weave the tunic with fine linen, make the turban of fine linen, and fashion an embroidered sash. (28:39).
Make tunics, sashes, and headbands for Aaron’s sons, to give them glory and splendor. (28:40).
After you put these garments on your brother Aaron and his sons, anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests. (28:41).
Make linen undergarments to cover their bare flesh, extending from waist to thigh. (28:42).

Aaron and his sons must wear them whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister in the Holy Place, so that they will not incur guilt and die. This is to be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants. (28:43).
crossRefs: Exodus 39:1-31: The same garments made piece by piece, each one just as the LORD commanded Moses.
Leviticus 8:6-9: Moses dresses Aaron in these garments and sets the turban and the gold plate on his head.
Numbers 27:21: Joshua is to stand before Eleazar, who will inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim.
1 Samuel 28:6: The LORD did not answer Saul by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets.
Ezra 2:63: Returning priests are barred from the most holy food until a priest can stand with Urim and Thummim.

translationNotes.note: The distance between thumb-tip and little-finger-tip with the fingers spread; half a cubit, about 9 inches (23 cm). The breastpiece of the high priest was a span square (Exodus 28:16).

An apron-like garment worn over the robe, joined at the shoulders and bound with a woven waistband. The high priest's was worked with gold thread and carried the breastpiece. A plain linen ephod was worn by others in priestly service, by Samuel in 1 Samuel 2:18 and by David in 2 Samuel 6:14.

A square of woven work, a span each way, about nine inches, folded double to make a pouch. Twelve engraved stones on the front named the tribes; the pouch held the Urim and Thummim. 'Judgment' names its function: this is where a decision was sought.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוּרִים וְתֻמִּים (Urim ve-Tummim), 'lights and perfections'
translationNotes.note: The means by which the high priest brought a question to God and received an answer. Numbers 27:21 has Joshua enquiring by them, 1 Samuel 28:6 records God refusing to answer Saul by them, and Ezra 2:63 shows them missing after the exile. Scripture never describes their shape or how they were worked.

A plate of pure gold engraved HOLY TO THE LORD and tied over the front of the turban with a blue cord. Exodus 28:38 says Aaron wore it so he would bear the guilt attached to Israel's holy gifts. It is the only piece of the priestly dress that carries writing.

Gold bells alternating with woollen pomegranates all round the hem of the blue robe. Exodus 28:35 gives the reason: the sound is heard when he enters and leaves the sanctuary, so that he will not die. The high priest was never to come and go silently.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses to have skilled workers make sacred garments for Aaron and his sons - an ephod with onyx stones bearing the names of Israel's tribes, a breastpiece set with twelve precious stones and holding the Urim and Thummim, a blue robe with pomegranates and gold bells, a gold plate inscribed "holy to the Lord," and fine linen tunics and undergarments. Aaron is to wear these garments when entering the Holy Place to bear the names of Israel before the Lord.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 29
summaryBullets: “Now this is what you are to do to consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests: Take a young bull and two rams without blemish, (29:1).
along with unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil. Make them out of fine wheat flour, (29:2).
put them in a basket, and present them in the basket, along with the bull and the two rams. (29:3).
Then present Aaron and his sons at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water. (29:4).
Take the garments and clothe Aaron with the tunic, the robe of the ephod, the ephod itself, and the breastplate. Fasten the ephod on him with its woven waistband. (29:5).
Put the turban on his head and attach the holy diadem to the turban. (29:6).
Then take the anointing oil and anoint him by pouring it on his head. (29:7).
Present his sons as well and clothe them with tunics. (29:8).
Wrap the sashes around Aaron and his sons and tie headbands on them. The priesthood shall be theirs by a permanent statute. In this way you are to ordain Aaron and his sons. (29:9).
You are to present the bull at the front of the Tent of Meeting, and Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on its head. (29:10).
And you shall slaughter the bull before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (29:11).
Take some of the blood of the bull and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger; then pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. (29:12).
Take all the fat that covers the entrails and the lobe of the liver, and both kidneys with the fat on them, and burn them on the altar. (29:13).
But burn the flesh of the bull and its hide and dung outside the camp; it is a sin offering. (29:14).
Take one of the rams, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on its head. (29:15).
You are to slaughter the ram, take its blood, and splatter it on all sides of the altar. (29:16).
Cut the ram into pieces, wash the entrails and legs, and place them with its head and other pieces. (29:17).
Then burn the entire ram on the altar; it is a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. (29:18).
Take the second ram, and Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on its head. (29:19).

Slaughter the ram, take some of its blood, and put it on the right earlobes of Aaron and his sons, on the thumbs of their right hands, and on the big toes of their right feet. Splatter the remaining blood on all sides of the altar. (29:20).

And take some of the blood on the altar and some of the anointing oil and sprinkle it on Aaron and his garments, as well as on his sons and their garments. Then he and his garments will be consecrated, as well as his sons and their garments. (29:21).
Take the fat from the ram, the fat tail, the fat covering the entrails, the lobe of the liver, both kidneys with the fat on them, and the right thigh (since this is a ram for ordination), (29:22).
along with one loaf of bread, one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer from the basket of unleavened bread that is before the LORD. (29:23).
Put all these in the hands of Aaron and his sons and wave them before the LORD as a wave offering. (29:24).
Then take them from their hands and burn them on the altar atop the burnt offering as a pleasing aroma before the LORD; it is a food offering to the LORD. (29:25).
Take the breast of the ram of Aaron’s ordination and wave it before the LORD as a wave offering, and it will be your portion. (29:26).
Consecrate for Aaron and his sons the breast of the wave offering that is waved and the thigh of the heave offering that is lifted up from the ram of ordination. (29:27).
This will belong to Aaron and his sons as a regular portion from the Israelites, for it is the heave offering the Israelites will make to the LORD from their peace offerings. (29:28).
The holy garments that belong to Aaron will belong to his sons after him, so they can be anointed and ordained in them. (29:29).
The son who succeeds him as priest and enters the Tent of Meeting to minister in the Holy Place must wear them for seven days. (29:30).
You are to take the ram of ordination and boil its flesh in a holy place. (29:31).
At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, Aaron and his sons are to eat the meat of the ram and the bread that is in the basket. (29:32).
They must eat those things by which atonement was made for their ordination and consecration. But no outsider may eat them, because these things are sacred. (29:33).
And if any of the meat of ordination or any bread is left until the morning, you are to burn up the remainder. It must not be eaten, because it is sacred. (29:34).
This is what you are to do for Aaron and his sons based on all that I have commanded you, taking seven days to ordain them. (29:35).
Sacrifice a bull as a sin offering each day for atonement. Purify the altar by making atonement for it, and anoint it to consecrate it. (29:36).
For seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it. Then the altar will become most holy; whatever touches the altar will be holy. (29:37).
This is what you are to offer regularly on the altar, each day: two lambs that are a year old. (29:38).
Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight. (29:39).
With the first lamb offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter hin of oil from pressed olives, and a drink offering of a quarter hin of wine. (29:40).
And offer the second lamb at twilight with the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning, as a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. (29:41).
For the generations to come, this burnt offering shall be made regularly at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, where I will meet you to speak with you. (29:42).
I will also meet with the Israelites there, and that place will be consecrated by My glory. (29:43).
So I will consecrate the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and I will consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests. (29:44).
Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God. (29:45).
And they will know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God. (29:46).
crossRefs: Leviticus 8:1-36: The ordination carried out over seven days exactly as it is commanded here.
Leviticus 7:28-34: The breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution assigned to the priests as a perpetual share.
Numbers 28:3-8: The daily burnt offering of two lambs restated with its flour, oil, and drink offering.
Exodus 40:12-15: Moses washes, clothes, and anoints Aaron and his sons at the entrance to the tent.
Hebrews 7:26-27: A high priest who has no need to offer sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins.

translationNotes.note: The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).
The standard temple liquid measure for wine and oil in offerings; about one gallon (3.8 liters). Used throughout Exodus and Numbers for prescribed drink offerings.

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִלֵּא יָד (mille yad), 'to fill the hand'
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew idiom for installing someone into an office is to fill his hand, and Exodus 29:24 acts it out: the portions are literally placed in Aaron's hands and waved. The same idiom appears in Exodus 32:29 and Judges 17:5. English 'ordain' hides the picture.

Two named motions with the portions: the tenufah was moved back and forth, the terumah lifted up and set aside as a contribution. Leviticus 7:30-34 makes the breast and the right thigh of every peace offering the priests' permanent share by these two acts.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּנוּךְ אֹזֶן, בֹּהֶן יָד, בֹּהֶן רֶגֶל (tenukh ozen, bohen yad, bohen regel)
translationNotes.note: Blood applied to the right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe of each priest. The identical three points are used again in Leviticus 14:14 when a healed leper is restored. It marks the extremities of hearing, doing, and going.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹלַת תָּמִיד (olat tamid), 'continual burnt offering'
translationNotes.note: Two year-old lambs a day, one at dawn and one at twilight, with flour, oil, and wine, restated in Numbers 28:3-8. This set the clock of Israel's worship; the hours of prayer in Acts 3:1 and Acts 10:3 follow the same rhythm. Daniel 8:11-13 measures desecration by its being taken away.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses is given detailed instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests through ritual washings, garment dressing, anointing, and animal sacrifices; the process takes seven days and establishes a daily offering routine at the tent of meeting.

headings.text: God Will Dwell among the People

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 30
summaryBullets: “You are also to make an altar of acacia wood for the burning of incense. (30:1).
It is to be square, a cubit long, a cubit wide, and two cubits high. Its horns must be of one piece. (30:2).
Overlay with pure gold the top and all the sides and horns, and make a molding of gold around it. (30:3).
And make two gold rings below the molding on opposite sides to hold the poles used to carry it. (30:4).
Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. (30:5).
Place the altar in front of the veil that is before the ark of the Testimony— before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony— where I will meet with you. (30:6).
And Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps. (30:7).
When Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he must burn the incense perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come. (30:8).
On this altar you must not offer unauthorized incense or a burnt offering or grain offering; nor are you to pour a drink offering on it. (30:9).

Once a year Aaron shall make atonement on the horns of the altar. Throughout your generations he shall make atonement on it annually with the blood of the sin offering of atonement. The altar is most holy to the LORD.” (30:10).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (30:11).
“When you take a census of the Israelites to number them, each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted. Then no plague will come upon them when they are numbered. (30:12).
Everyone who crosses over to those counted must pay a half shekel, according to the sanctuary shekel, which weighs twenty gerahs. This half shekel is an offering to the LORD. (30:13).
Everyone twenty years of age or older who crosses over must give this offering to the LORD. (30:14).
In making the offering to the LORD to atone for your lives, the rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less. (30:15).

Take the atonement money from the Israelites and use it for the service of the Tent of Meeting. It will serve as a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD to make atonement for your lives.” (30:16).
And the LORD said to Moses, (30:17).
“You are to make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. Set it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and put water in it, (30:18).
with which Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet. (30:19).
Whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister by presenting a food offering to the LORD, they must wash with water so that they will not die. (30:20).
Thus they are to wash their hands and feet so that they will not die; this shall be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants for the generations to come.” (30:21).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (30:22).
“Take the finest spices: 500 shekels of liquid myrrh, half that amount (250 shekels) of fragrant cinnamon, 250 shekels of fragrant cane, (30:23).
500 shekels of cassia — all according to the sanctuary shekel — and a hin of olive oil. (30:24).
Prepare from these a sacred anointing oil, a fragrant blend, the work of a perfumer; it will be a sacred anointing oil. (30:25).
Use this oil to anoint the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the Testimony, (30:26).
the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense, (30:27).
the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the basin with its stand. (30:28).
You are to consecrate them so that they will be most holy. Whatever touches them shall be holy. (30:29).
Anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve Me as priests. (30:30).
And you are to tell the Israelites, ‘This will be My sacred anointing oil for the generations to come. (30:31).
It must not be used to anoint an ordinary man, and you must not make anything like it with the same formula. It is holy, and it must be holy to you. (30:32).
Anyone who mixes perfume like it or puts it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.’” (30:33).
The LORD also said to Moses, “Take fragrant spices — gum resin, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense — in equal measures, (30:34).
and make a fragrant blend of incense, the work of a perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy. (30:35).
Grind some of it into fine powder and place it in front of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting, where I will meet with you. It shall be most holy to you. (30:36).
You are never to use this formula to make incense for yourselves; you shall regard it as holy to the LORD. (30:37).
Anyone who makes something like it to enjoy its fragrance shall be cut off from his people.” (30:38).
crossRefs: Exodus 38:25-28: The silver from this half-shekel count weighed out and used for the bases of the sanctuary.
Numbers 16:16-18: Korah and his company each take a censer, put fire and incense in it, and stand at the tent entrance.
Luke 1:8-11: Zechariah is chosen by lot to burn incense while the whole assembly prays outside.
Revelation 8:3-4: An angel offers much incense with the prayers of the saints on the golden altar before the throne.
Matthew 17:24-27: Collectors of the two-drachma temple tax ask Peter whether his teacher pays it.

translationNotes.note: The smallest Hebrew weight unit; twenty gerahs equal one shekel (Exodus 30:13). Approximately half a gram in modern measure.

The distance from elbow to fingertip; about 18 inches (45 cm). The standard biblical measure for buildings (Noah's ark, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple) and bodies. Goliath was 'six cubits and a span' tall, about 9 feet 9 in. A 'long cubit' (Ezekiel 40:5) added a handbreadth.
The standard temple liquid measure for wine and oil in offerings; about one gallon (3.8 liters). Used throughout Exodus and Numbers for prescribed drink offerings.

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

A fragrant gum resin from the Commiphora tree of Arabia and East Africa. Used as a holy anointing-oil ingredient (Exodus 30:23), as perfume, as an embalming spice (John 19:39), and, mixed with wine, as a pain-dulling drink (Mark 15:23). One of the magi's gifts.

A milky-white resin from the Boswellia tree of southern Arabia. Burned as incense in the temple (Exodus 30:34); offered with every grain offering. The magi's second gift, traditionally read as signaling priesthood.

Both a weight (about 0.4 oz / 11 g) and a currency unit. In Old Testament economy a common laborer earned roughly half a shekel per month, so the 20 shekels paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28) was about three years of wages. The temple tax was half a shekel (Exodus 30:13); in New Testament reckoning that equaled two denarii / two days' wages.

The reference weight kept at the sanctuary, about 11.4 grams of silver, divided into twenty gerahs. Exodus 38:25-26 lets you check the larger unit: 603,550 half shekels come to 100 talents plus 1,775 shekels, so a talent is exactly 3,000 shekels, about 34 kilograms or 75 pounds.

About 5.7 grams of silver, and the same sum from rich and poor alike (Exodus 30:15). By the first century this had become the annual temple tax, paid as a two-drachma coin; Matthew 17:24-27 is about that payment.

A washing stand set between the altar and the tent, for the priests' hands and feet. Exodus 38:8 records what it was made from: the bronze mirrors of the women who served at the tent entrance. Ancient mirrors were discs of polished bronze, which is the image behind 1 Corinthians 13:12.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָר־דְּרוֹר, קִנְּמָן־בֶּשֶׂם, קְנֵה־בֹשֶׂם, קִדָּה (mor-deror, qinnemon-besem, qeneh-vosem, qiddah)
translationNotes.note: By weight: 500 shekels of liquid myrrh, 250 of cinnamon, 250 of fragrant cane, 500 of cassia, with a hin of olive oil. In modern terms that is about 5.7 kilograms of myrrh and of cassia, 2.85 kilograms each of the other two, in roughly one gallon of oil. Every one of the spices had to be imported.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָטָף, שְׁחֵלֶת, חֶלְבְּנָה, לְבֹנָה (nataf, shecheleth, chelbenah, levonah)
translationNotes.note: Four ingredients in equal weights. Nataf is a drop of gum resin; chelbenah is galbanum, a bitter resin from a Ferula plant of Persia; levonah is frankincense. Shecheleth, onycha, is not identified anywhere in Scripture. Copying the blend for private use carried the penalty of being cut off (Exodus 30:38).

A fixed legal formula, karet, running through Exodus and Leviticus for the gravest offences. It removes a person from the covenant community and its protections rather than naming a court penalty. Genesis 17:14 applies it to the uncircumcised.

translationNotes.term: do not make this for yourselves
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּרַת מֵעַמָּיו (karat me-ammav), cut off from his people
translationNotes.note: Both formulas in this chapter, the anointing oil and the incense, are closed. Exodus 30:32-33 forbids putting the oil on an ordinary person or copying the blend, and 30:37-38 forbids making the incense to enjoy the smell of it; the penalty for either is being cut off from the people. Perfumery was a valuable trade and these were expensive materials, so the ban keeps a commercial industry from growing on the sanctuary's recipe.

stories.keyTakeaway: God gives instructions for an incense altar, a census tax of half a shekel per person, a bronze basin for washing, and formulas for sacred anointing oil and incense that are reserved for priestly use only.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 31
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (31:1).
“See, I have called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. (31:2).
And I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship, (31:3).
to design artistic works in gold, silver, and bronze, (31:4).
to cut gemstones for settings, and to carve wood, so that he may be a master of every craft. (31:5).
Moreover, I have selected Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, as his assistant. I have also given skill to all the craftsmen, that they may fashion all that I have commanded you: (31:6).
the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the Testimony and the mercy seat upon it, and all the other furnishings of the tent— (31:7).
the table with its utensils, the pure gold lampstand with all its utensils, the altar of incense, (31:8).
the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin with its stand— (31:9).
as well as the woven garments, both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests, (31:10).
in addition to the anointing oil and fragrant incense for the Holy Place. They are to make them according to all that I have commanded you.” (31:11).
And the LORD said to Moses, (31:12).
“Tell the Israelites, ‘Surely you must keep My Sabbaths, for this will be a sign between Me and you for the generations to come, so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you. (31:13).
Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you. Anyone who profanes it must surely be put to death. Whoever does any work on that day must be cut off from among his people. (31:14).
For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day must surely be put to death. (31:15).
The Israelites must keep the Sabbath, celebrating it as a permanent covenant for the generations to come. (31:16).
It is a sign between Me and the Israelites forever; for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed.’” (31:17).
When the LORD had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him the two tablets of the Testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God. (31:18).
crossRefs: Exodus 35:30-35: Bezalel and Oholiab named again, and given the ability to teach others their craft.
1 Kings 7:13-14: Huram of Tyre, filled with skill, understanding, and knowledge for all bronze work.
Ezekiel 20:12: I also gave them My Sabbaths as a sign between Me and them.
Numbers 15:32-36: A man found gathering wood on the Sabbath day is put to death at the LORD's word.
Deuteronomy 9:10: The LORD gave Moses two stone tablets inscribed by the finger of God.

translationNotes.note: Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

translationNotes.term: filled with the Spirit of God
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וָאֲמַלֵּא אֹתוֹ רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים (va-amalle oto ruach elohim)
translationNotes.note: Exodus 31:3 is the first place in Scripture where anyone is said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and the gift named is craftsmanship: metalwork, stonecutting, carpentry, design. Bezalel is from Judah and Oholiab from Dan, two different tribes working the same commission.

translationNotes.term: a sign between Me and you
translationNotes.note: The Sabbath is called a sign in the same sense as the rainbow in Genesis 9:13 and circumcision in Genesis 17:11: a public marker of a covenant. Ezekiel 20:12 repeats the term. Exodus 31:17 grounds it in the six days of creation, not in the Exodus.

Two stone tablets written on both sides (Exodus 32:15). Treaties in the ancient Near East were commonly issued in duplicate, one copy for each party, and both copies of this one were placed in the ark. Deuteronomy 10:1-5 records where they were kept.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD designates Bezalel and Oholiab to oversee construction of the tabernacle and its furnishings, empowering all skilled workers to complete the project. God also commands the Israelites to observe the Sabbath as a lasting covenant, prescribing death for those who work on that day; Moses then receives the two stone tablets inscribed by God's finger.

stories.title: 🐂 Exodus 32
summaryBullets: Now when the people saw that Moses was delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron and said, “Come, make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him!” (32:1).
So Aaron told them, “Take off the gold earrings that are on your wives and sons and daughters, and bring them to me.” (32:2).
Then all the people took off their gold earrings and brought them to Aaron. (32:3).
He took the gold from their hands, and with an engraving tool he fashioned it into a molten calf. And they said, “These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” (32:4).
When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before the calf and proclaimed: “Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD.” (32:5).
So the next day they arose, offered burnt offerings, and presented peace offerings. And the people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry. (32:6).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go down at once, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves. (32:7).

How quickly they have turned aside from the way that I commanded them! They have made for themselves a molten calf and have bowed down to it. They have sacrificed to it and said, ‘These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.’” (32:8).
The LORD also said to Moses, “I have seen this people, and they are indeed a stiff-necked people. (32:9).
Now leave Me alone, so that My anger may burn against them and consume them. Then I will make you into a great nation.” (32:10).
But Moses sought the favor of the LORD his God, saying, “O LORD, why does Your anger burn against Your people, whom You brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and a mighty hand? (32:11).

Why should the Egyptians declare, ‘He brought them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and wipe them from the face of the earth’? Turn from Your fierce anger and relent from doing harm to Your people. (32:12).

Remember Your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, to whom You swore by Your very self when You declared, ‘I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, and I will give your descendants all this land that I have promised, and it shall be their inheritance forever.’” (32:13).
So the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened to bring on His people. (32:14).
Then Moses turned and went down the mountain with the two tablets of the Testimony in his hands. They were inscribed on both sides, front and back. (32:15).
The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets. (32:16).
When Joshua heard the sound of the people shouting, he said to Moses, “The sound of war is in the camp.” (32:17).
But Moses replied: “It is neither the cry of victory nor the cry of defeat; I hear the sound of singing!” (32:18).
As Moses approached the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, he burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain. (32:19).
Then he took the calf they had made, burned it in the fire, ground it to powder, and scattered the powder over the face of the water. Then he forced the Israelites to drink it. (32:20).
“What did this people do to you,” Moses asked Aaron, “that you have led them into so great a sin?” (32:21).
“Do not be enraged, my lord,” Aaron replied. “You yourself know that the people are intent on evil. (32:22).
They told me, ‘Make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him!’ (32:23).
So I said to them, ‘Whoever has gold, let him take it off,’ and they gave it to me. And when I threw it into the fire, out came this calf!” (32:24).
Moses saw that the people were out of control, for Aaron had let them run wild and become a laughingstock to their enemies. (32:25).
So Moses stood at the entrance to the camp and said, “Whoever is for the LORD, come to me.” And all the Levites gathered around him. (32:26).

He told them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Each of you men is to fasten his sword to his side, go back and forth through the camp from gate to gate, and slay his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.’” (32:27).
The Levites did as Moses commanded, and that day about three thousand of the people fell dead. (32:28).
Afterward, Moses said, “Today you have been ordained for service to the LORD, since each man went against his son and his brother; so the LORD has bestowed a blessing on you this day.” (32:29).
The next day Moses said to the people, “You have committed a great sin. Now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin.” (32:30).
So Moses returned to the LORD and said, “Oh, what a great sin these people have committed! They have made gods of gold for themselves. (32:31).
Yet now, if You would only forgive their sin.... But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written.” (32:32).
The LORD replied to Moses, “Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot out of My book. (32:33).
Now go, lead the people to the place I described. Behold, My angel shall go before you. But on the day I settle accounts, I will punish them for their sin.” (32:34).
And the LORD sent a plague on the people because of what they had done with the calf that Aaron had made. (32:35).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 12:26-30: Jeroboam sets up two golden calves and repeats these same words to Israel.
Acts 7:39-41: Stephen recounts Israel turning back to Egypt in their hearts and making a calf.
Psalm 106:19-23: They made a calf at Horeb, and Moses stood in the breach to turn away God's wrath.
Deuteronomy 9:15-21: Moses recounts breaking the tablets, burning the calf, and grinding it to dust.
1 Corinthians 10:6-8: These things happened as examples; do not be idolaters as some of them were.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר (sefer), a written document - מָחָה (machah), to wipe out
translationNotes.note: Moses offers at 32:32 to be blotted out of the book God has written, and 32:33 answers that whoever has sinned will be blotted out of it. A sefer is any written document, and cities kept registers of citizens; Nehemiah 7:5 and Ezra 2:62 show such rolls being consulted, and men who could not prove their line were struck off. Psalm 69:28, Daniel 12:1 and Revelation 3:5 all use the same image of a register with names in it.

A young bull, cast from metal. Egypt kept living sacred bulls, Apis at Memphis and Mnevis at Heliopolis, and the bull was the standard image of strength in Canaanite religion as well. Jeroboam repeats the exact words of Exodus 32:4 over his two calves in 1 Kings 12:28.

The verb tsachaq means to laugh or to sport, the same root behind Isaac's name in Genesis 21:6 and used of Isaac caressing Rebekah in Genesis 26:8. Paul quotes this line in 1 Corinthians 10:7. The English 'revelry' is a fair guess at what the Hebrew leaves blunt.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִלְאוּ יֶדְכֶם (mil'u yedkhem), 'fill your hands'
translationNotes.note: The same idiom used for installing priests in Exodus 29:9. Exodus 32:29 uses it of the Levites after they act, and Numbers 3:11-13 records the tribe being taken for tabernacle service in place of Israel's firstborn.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵלֶּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל (elleh elohekha Yisrael), these are your gods, Israel
translationNotes.note: The cry the people raise over the calf in Exodus 32:4 turns up again, nearly word for word, when Jeroboam sets up two golden calves at Bethel and Dan and tells the northern kingdom not to go up to Jerusalem: 1 Kings 12:28. The bull was the standard image of strength in the religions on both sides of Israel, sacred bulls kept in Egypt at Memphis and Heliopolis and the bull used for El and Baal in Canaan. Neither Aaron nor Jeroboam announces a new god; both attach the name of the LORD to an image (32:5).

stories.keyTakeaway: While Moses receives the stone tablets on the mountain, the Israelites pressure Aaron to make a golden calf idol, which they worship with sacrifices and revelry; Moses intercedes with God to spare them, then breaks the tablets in anger, destroys the calf, and orders the Levites to kill about three thousand people.

stories.title: 🐂 Exodus 33
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Leave this place, you and the people you brought up out of the land of Egypt, and go to the land that I promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when I said, ‘I will give it to your descendants.’ (33:1).
And I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. (33:2).
Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey. But I will not go with you, because you are a stiff-necked people; otherwise, I might destroy you on the way.” (33:3).
When the people heard this bad news, they went into mourning, and no one put on any of his jewelry. (33:4).

For the LORD had said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites, ‘You are a stiff-necked people. If I should go with you for a single moment, I would destroy you. Now take off your jewelry, and I will decide what to do with you.’” (33:5).
So the Israelites stripped themselves of their jewelry from Mount Horeb onward. (33:6).

Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it at a distance outside the camp. He called it the Tent of Meeting, and anyone inquiring of the LORD would go to the Tent of Meeting outside the camp. (33:7).
Then, whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would stand at the entrances to their own tents and watch Moses until he entered the tent. (33:8).
As Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would come down and remain at the entrance, and the LORD would speak with Moses. (33:9).
When all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance to the tent, they would stand up and worship, each one at the entrance to his own tent. (33:10).
Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Then Moses would return to the camp, but his young assistant Joshua son of Nun would not leave the tent. (33:11).

Then Moses said to the LORD, “Look, You have been telling me, ‘Lead this people up,’ but You have not let me know whom You will send with me. Yet You have said, ‘I know you by name, and you have found favor in My sight.’ (33:12).
Now if indeed I have found favor in Your sight, please let me know Your ways, that I may know You and find favor in Your sight. Remember that this nation is Your people.” (33:13).
And the LORD answered, “My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.” (33:14).
“If Your Presence does not go with us,” Moses replied, “do not lead us up from here. (33:15).

For how then can it be known that Your people and I have found favor in Your sight, unless You go with us? How else will we be distinguished from all the other people on the face of the earth?” (33:16).
So the LORD said to Moses, “I will do this very thing you have asked, for you have found favor in My sight, and I know you by name.” (33:17).
Then Moses said, “Please show me Your glory.” (33:18).
