“I will cause all My goodness to pass before you,” the LORD replied, “and I will proclaim My name — the LORD — in your presence. I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” (33:19).
But He added, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live.” (33:20).
The LORD continued, “There is a place near Me where you are to stand upon a rock, (33:21).
and when My glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with My hand until I have passed by. (33:22).
Then I will take My hand away, and you will see My back; but My face must not be seen.” (33:23).
crossRefs: Numbers 12:6-8: With Moses the LORD speaks mouth to mouth, plainly and not in riddles.
Deuteronomy 34:10: No prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face.
1 Kings 19:11-13: The LORD passes by Elijah at Horeb while he stands at the mouth of the cave.
John 1:18: No one has ever seen God; the only Son, who is at the Father's side, has made Him known.
Romans 9:15: Paul quotes this chapter, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּבוֹד (kavod), from a root meaning heavy - טוּב (tuv), goodness
translationNotes.note: Moses asks to see God's kavod at 33:18, and the answer at 33:19 substitutes something else: all My goodness will pass before you and I will proclaim the name of the LORD. What is granted is a proclamation and a passing view from behind (33:23); what is refused at 33:20 is the face, because no man may see it and live. The proclamation itself is then made at 34:6-7.

Moed means an appointed time or appointed place, the same word used for the appointed feasts in Leviticus 23:2. So the name says what the tent is for: a fixed place of appointment with God. The tent of Exodus 33:7 is pitched outside the camp, before the tabernacle itself is built.

An idiom for direct, unmediated dealing, as one man speaks with a friend. It is not a claim to have seen God's face; Exodus 33:20 rules that out three verses after using the phrase. Numbers 12:8 says the same thing another way, mouth to mouth and not in riddles.

A crevice or fissure in the rock face. Elijah is put in the same position at the same mountain in 1 Kings 19:9-13, standing at the mouth of a cave while the LORD passes by. Exodus 33:22 has God's own hand as the cover.

Verses 33:4-6 are the aftermath of the calf. The people go into mourning at the news that God will not travel with them, take off their ornaments, and 33:6 notes they went without them from Horeb onward. Jewelry is what the calf was made of (32:2-3), and taking it off is the recognised sign of mourning in that world, alongside tearing clothes and sitting in ashes (Genesis 37:34; Job 2:12).

stories.keyTakeaway: God tells Moses to lead the people to the promised land but will not go with them due to their stiff-necked nature; the people mourn and remove their ornaments. Moses meets with God at a tent outside camp, argues that God's presence is necessary to distinguish Israel from other nations, and God agrees to go with them; Moses then requests to see God's glory, and God permits him to see his back while sheltered in a rock cleft, since no one can see God's face and live.

stories.title: 🐂 Exodus 34
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, and I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke. (34:1).
Be ready in the morning, and come up on Mount Sinai to present yourself before Me on the mountaintop. (34:2).
No one may go up with you; in fact, no one may be seen anywhere on the mountain — not even the flocks or herds may graze in front of the mountain.” (34:3).
So Moses chiseled out two stone tablets like the originals. He rose early in the morning, and taking the two stone tablets in his hands, he went up Mount Sinai as the LORD had commanded him. (34:4).
And the LORD descended in a cloud, stood with him there, and proclaimed His name, the LORD. (34:5).
Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, (34:6).

maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished; He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generations.” (34:7).
Moses immediately bowed down to the ground and worshiped. (34:8).

“O Lord,” he said, “if I have indeed found favor in Your sight, my Lord, please go with us. Although this is a stiff-necked people, forgive our iniquity and sin, and take us as Your inheritance.” (34:9).

And the LORD said, “Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will perform wonders that have never been done in any nation in all the world. All the people among whom you live will see the LORD’s work, for it is an awesome thing that I am doing with you. (34:10).
Observe what I command you this day. I will drive out before you the Amorites, Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. (34:11).
Be careful not to make a treaty with the inhabitants of the land you are entering, lest they become a snare in your midst. (34:12).
Rather, you must tear down their altars, smash their sacred stones, and chop down their Asherah poles. (34:13).
For you must not worship any other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God. (34:14).
Do not make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, for when they prostitute themselves to their gods and sacrifice to them, they will invite you, and you will eat their sacrifices. (34:15).
And when you take some of their daughters as brides for your sons, their daughters will prostitute themselves to their gods and cause your sons to do the same. (34:16).
You shall make no molten gods for yourselves. (34:17).

You are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, you are to eat unleavened bread as I commanded you. For in the month of Abib you came out of Egypt. (34:18).
The first offspring of every womb belongs to Me, including all the firstborn males among your livestock, whether cattle or sheep. (34:19).

You must redeem the firstborn of a donkey with a lamb; but if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck. You must redeem all the firstborn of your sons. No one shall appear before Me empty-handed. (34:20).
Six days you shall labor, but on the seventh day you shall rest; even in the seasons of plowing and harvesting, you must rest. (34:21).
And you are to celebrate the Feast of Weeks with the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering at the turn of the year. (34:22).
Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel. (34:23).
For I will drive out the nations before you and enlarge your borders, and no one will covet your land when you go up three times a year to appear before the LORD your God. (34:24).
Do not offer the blood of a sacrifice to Me along with anything leavened, and do not let any of the sacrifice from the Passover Feast remain until morning. (34:25).
Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk.” (34:26).
The LORD also said to Moses, “Write down these words, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.” (34:27).
So Moses was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights without eating bread or drinking water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant — the Ten Commandments. (34:28).
And when Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the Testimony in his hands, he was unaware that his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD. (34:29).
Aaron and all the Israelites looked at Moses, and behold, his face was radiant. And they were afraid to approach him. (34:30).
But Moses called out to them; so Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses spoke to them. (34:31).
And after this all the Israelites came near, and Moses commanded them to do everything that the LORD had told him on Mount Sinai. (34:32).
When Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face. (34:33).
But whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with Him, he would remove the veil until he came out. And when he came out, he would tell the Israelites what he had been commanded, (34:34).
and the Israelites would see that the face of Moses was radiant. So Moses would put the veil back over his face until he went in to speak with the LORD. (34:35).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 10:1-5: Moses recounts cutting two new tablets and placing them in the ark he had made.
Numbers 14:18: Moses prays back to God the words proclaimed here, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion.
Psalm 103:8: The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion.
Jonah 4:2: Jonah quotes the same formula as his reason for running from Nineveh.
2 Corinthians 3:7-16: Paul writes of the veil over Moses' face and the glory that was passing away.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַנָּא (qanna) - שְׁמוֹ קַנָּא (shemo qanna), 'His name is Jealous'
translationNotes.note: Verse 34:14 goes further than 20:5: it makes Jealous a name, not just a description. Qanna is used in Scripture only of God, and the ordinary human use of the root is a husband's response to a wife's unfaithfulness, which is exactly the picture 34:15-16 draws when it warns that Israel will prostitute themselves to the gods of the land. It is not envy, which wants what belongs to someone else; it is a claim on what is already one's own.

The first portion of each harvest offered to God before the rest could be eaten (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:9-14). Paul calls the resurrected Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20); the guarantee that the full resurrection harvest will follow.

The verb means to send out rays, but it is built on the noun for a horn. Jerome's Latin Vulgate, finished about 405 AD, rendered it cornuta, horned, and that reading is why Michelangelo's Moses of 1513-1515 has horns on his head. The Hebrew describes light, not horns.

Wooden cult objects standing beside Canaanite altars, named for the goddess Asherah. They were planted or set upright, which is why the command is to cut them down (Deuteronomy 7:5; 2 Kings 23:6). Exodus 34:13 pairs them with altars and sacred stones as the three things to destroy.

An upright standing stone. Jacob sets one up as a marker at Bethel in Genesis 28:18, but the same object serving a Canaanite altar is banned outright here and in Leviticus 26:1. Rows of such standing stones have been excavated at Canaanite sites including Gezer and Hazor.

translationNotes.term: The LORD, the LORD, compassionate and gracious
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן (rachum vechannun) - חֶסֶד (chesed), loyal covenant love
translationNotes.note: The sentence God proclaims over Moses at 34:6-7 becomes the most quoted description of God in the Hebrew Bible. Israel quotes it back at Numbers 14:18, the Levites recite it at Nehemiah 9:17, and it turns up at Psalm 86:15, 103:8 and 145:8, Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2. Rachum is built on the word for a womb; chesed is loyalty inside a covenant rather than affection. Nahum 1:3 opens with the same formula and carries it in the other direction, that He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses receives two new stone tablets and spends forty days on Mount Sinai, where God proclaims his character, renews the covenant, and gives instructions on worship and festivals. When Moses descends with the covenant written on the tablets, his face radiates from speaking with God, causing the Israelites to fear him until he speaks to them and covers his face with a veil.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 35
summaryBullets: Then Moses assembled the whole congregation of Israel and said to them, “These are the things that the LORD has commanded you to do: (35:1).
For six days work may be done, but the seventh day shall be your holy day, a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD. Whoever does any work on that day must be put to death. (35:2).
Do not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day.” (35:3).
Moses also told the whole congregation of Israel, “This is what the LORD has commanded: (35:4).
Take from among you an offering to the LORD. Let everyone whose heart is willing bring an offering to the LORD: gold, silver, and bronze; (35:5).
blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair; (35:6).
ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood; (35:7).
olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense; (35:8).
and onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece. (35:9).
Let every skilled craftsman among you come and make everything that the LORD has commanded: (35:10).
the tabernacle with its tent and covering, its clasps and frames, its crossbars, posts, and bases; (35:11).
the ark with its poles and mercy seat, and the veil to shield it; (35:12).
the table with its poles, all its utensils, and the Bread of the Presence; (35:13).
the lampstand for light with its accessories and lamps and oil for the light; (35:14).
the altar of incense with its poles; the anointing oil and fragrant incense; the curtain for the doorway at the entrance to the tabernacle; (35:15).
the altar of burnt offering with its bronze grate, its poles, and all its utensils; the basin with its stand; (35:16).
the curtains of the courtyard with its posts and bases, and the curtain for the gate of the courtyard; (35:17).
the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the courtyard, along with their ropes; (35:18).
and the woven garments for ministering in the holy place— both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests.” (35:19).
Then the whole congregation of Israel withdrew from the presence of Moses. (35:20).

And everyone whose heart stirred him and whose spirit prompted him came and brought an offering to the LORD for the work on the Tent of Meeting, for all its services, and for the holy garments. (35:21).

So all who had willing hearts, both men and women, came and brought brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry. And they all presented their gold as a wave offering to the LORD. (35:22).
Everyone who had blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, or fine linen, goat hair, ram skins dyed red, or articles of fine leather, brought them. (35:23).
And all who could present an offering of silver or bronze brought it as a contribution to the LORD. Also, everyone who had acacia wood for any part of the service brought it. (35:24).
Every skilled woman spun with her hands and brought what she had spun: blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, or fine linen. (35:25).
And all the skilled women whose hearts were stirred spun the goat hair. (35:26).
The leaders brought onyx stones and gemstones to mount on the ephod and breastpiece, (35:27).
as well as spices and olive oil for the light, for the anointing oil, and for the fragrant incense. (35:28).
So all the men and women of the Israelites whose hearts prompted them brought a freewill offering to the LORD for all the work that the LORD through Moses had commanded them to do. (35:29).
Then Moses said to the Israelites, “See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. (35:30).
And He has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship, (35:31).
to design artistic works in gold, silver, and bronze, (35:32).
to cut gemstones for settings, and to carve wood, so that he may be a master of every artistic craft. (35:33).
And the LORD has given both him and Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, the ability to teach others. (35:34).

He has filled them with skill to do all kinds of work as engravers, designers, embroiderers in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, and as weavers — as artistic designers of every kind of craft. (35:35).
crossRefs: Exodus 25:1-9: The same list of materials first requested for the sanctuary.
1 Chronicles 29:1-9: Israel's leaders give willingly for the temple, and the people rejoice at their freewill offering.
Ezra 2:68-69: Heads of families give freewill offerings toward rebuilding the house of God on its site.
Numbers 15:32-36: A man found gathering wood on the Sabbath day, the command of verse 3 tested in the camp.
2 Corinthians 9:7: Each should give what he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion.

translationNotes.note: A voluntary contribution given willingly, not by obligation.

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

Kindling was work: gathering fuel, striking a light, tending it. Exodus 16:23 had already told Israel to bake and boil on the sixth day. Numbers 15:32-36 records what happened to a man found gathering wood on the Sabbath in this same wilderness.

Spinning was done on a drop spindle, a weighted shaft twirled by hand, and goat hair is coarse and greasy to work. Exodus 35:25-26 credits the women with spinning both the fine dyed wool and the goat hair, so the outer tent and the inner curtains alike came off their spindles.

Brooches, earrings, rings, and necklaces, presented with the same waving motion used for the priests' portions in Exodus 29:24. This is the metal Israel carried out of Egypt (Exodus 12:35), and the same kind of jewelry that had gone into the calf in Exodus 32:2-3.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses instructs Israel to observe the Sabbath and calls for voluntary offerings of materials and skilled labor to build the tabernacle; the people respond by bringing gold, silver, bronze, yarn, leather, wood, stones, and spices, and Moses identifies Bezalel and Oholiab as divinely gifted craftsmen to oversee the work.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 36
summaryBullets: “So Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person are to carry out everything commanded by the LORD, who has given them skill and ability to know how to perform all the work of constructing the sanctuary.” (36:1).
Then Moses summoned Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person whom the LORD had gifted — everyone whose heart stirred him to come and do the work. (36:2).

They received from Moses all the contributions that the Israelites had brought to carry out the service of constructing the sanctuary. Meanwhile, the people continued to bring freewill offerings morning after morning, (36:3).
so that all the skilled craftsmen who were doing all the work on the sanctuary left their work (36:4).
and said to Moses, “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do.” (36:5).

After Moses had given an order, they sent a proclamation throughout the camp: “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary.” So the people were restrained from bringing more, (36:6).
since what they already had was more than enough to perform all the work. (36:7).

All the skilled craftsmen among the workmen made the ten curtains for the tabernacle. They were made of finely spun linen, as well as blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with cherubim skillfully worked into them. (36:8).
Each curtain was twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide; all the curtains were the same size. (36:9).
And he joined five of the curtains together, and the other five he joined as well. (36:10).
He made loops of blue material on the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and also on the end curtain in the second set. (36:11).
He made fifty loops on one curtain and fifty loops on the end curtain of the second set, so that the loops lined up opposite one another. (36:12).
He also made fifty gold clasps to join the curtains together, so that the tabernacle was a unit. (36:13).
He then made curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle — eleven curtains in all. (36:14).
Each of the eleven curtains was the same size — thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. (36:15).
He joined five of the curtains into one set and the other six into another. (36:16).
He made fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and fifty loops along the edge of the corresponding curtain in the second set. (36:17).
He also made fifty bronze clasps to join the tent together as a unit. (36:18).
Additionally, he made for the tent a covering of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather. (36:19).
Next, he constructed upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle. (36:20).
Each frame was ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. (36:21).
Two tenons were connected to each other for each frame. He made all the frames of the tabernacle in this way. (36:22).
He constructed twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle, (36:23).
with forty silver bases to put under the twenty frames — two bases for each frame, one under each tenon. (36:24).
For the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, he made twenty frames (36:25).
and forty silver bases — two bases under each frame. (36:26).
He made six frames for the rear of the tabernacle, the west side, (36:27).
and two frames for the two back corners of the tabernacle, (36:28).
coupled together from bottom to top and fitted into a single ring. He made both corners in this way. (36:29).
So there were eight frames and sixteen silver bases — two under each frame. (36:30).
He also made five crossbars of acacia wood for the frames on one side of the tabernacle, (36:31).
five for those on the other side, and five for those on the rear side of the tabernacle, to the west. (36:32).
He made the central crossbar to run through the center of the frames, from one end to the other. (36:33).
And he overlaid the frames with gold and made gold rings to hold the crossbars. He also overlaid the crossbars with gold. (36:34).
Next, he made the veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it. (36:35).
He also made four posts of acacia wood for it and overlaid them with gold, along with gold hooks; and he cast four silver bases for the posts. (36:36).
For the entrance to the tent, he made a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, (36:37).
together with five posts and their hooks. He overlaid the tops of the posts and their bands with gold, and their five bases were bronze. (36:38).
crossRefs: Exodus 26:1-37: The instructions these workmen are following, curtain by curtain and frame by frame.
1 Chronicles 22:15-16: Stonecutters, masons, carpenters, and craftsmen without number prepared for the temple work.
2 Kings 12:9-16: Money brought into the house of the LORD is paid straight to the workmen, who deal honestly.
2 Chronicles 24:8-14: A chest set at the gate collects money for repairs until the work is done and a surplus is left.
Haggai 1:7-8: Go up to the hills, bring down timber, and build the house, says the LORD.

translationNotes.note: A voluntary contribution given willingly, not by obligation.

The distance from elbow to fingertip; about 18 inches (45 cm). The standard biblical measure for buildings (Noah's ark, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple) and bodies. Goliath was 'six cubits and a span' tall, about 9 feet 9 in. A 'long cubit' (Ezekiel 40:5) added a handbreadth.

Exodus 36:5-7 is the only place in Scripture where a collection has to be stopped by proclamation. The craftsmen themselves brought the complaint. The totals are given later in Exodus 38:24-29: about a metric ton of gold, three and a half of silver, two and a half of bronze.

Five horizontal bars per wall, running through gold rings on the frames, with the middle one running the full length from end to end. They are what turns forty-eight separate frames into one rigid structure that can still be taken apart in an hour. Numbers 4:31-32 assigns them to the Merarites to carry.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses gathers the skilled workers and receives offerings from the people; the workers report having more than enough materials, so Moses halts further contributions. The skilled workers then construct the tabernacle's curtains, frames, crossbars, and posts according to the specifications, overlaying wood with gold and bronze.

headings.text: The People Bring More than Enough
The Ten Curtains for the Tabernacle
The Eleven Curtains of Goat Hair

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 37
summaryBullets: Bezalel went on to construct the ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. (37:1).
He overlaid it with pure gold, both inside and out, and made a gold molding around it. (37:2).
And he cast four gold rings for its four feet, two rings on one side and two on the other. (37:3).
Then he made poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. (37:4).
He inserted the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark in order to carry it. (37:5).

He made two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat, (37:7).
one cherub on one end and one on the other, all made from one piece of gold. (37:8).
And the cherubim had wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat. The cherubim faced each other, looking toward the mercy seat. (37:9).
He also made the table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. (37:10).
He overlaid it with pure gold and made a gold molding around it. (37:11).
And he made a rim around it a handbreadth wide and put a gold molding on the rim. (37:12).
He cast four gold rings for the table and fastened them to the four corners at its four legs. (37:13).
The rings were placed close to the rim, to serve as holders for the poles used to carry the table. (37:14).
He made the poles of acacia wood for carrying the table and overlaid them with gold. (37:15).
He also made the utensils for the table out of pure gold: its plates and dishes, as well as its bowls and pitchers for pouring drink offerings. (37:16).

Six branches extended from the sides, three on one side and three on the other. (37:18).

translationNotes.note: The distance from elbow to fingertip; about 18 inches (45 cm). The standard biblical measure for buildings (Noah's ark, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple) and bodies. The width of four fingers, about 3 inches (7.5 cm). Used for small dimensions on temple furniture and as a metaphor for the brevity of life (Psalm 39:5).

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

Worked from a single mass of metal by hammering, with nothing cast, joined, or soldered on. The lampstand and the two cherubim of the mercy seat were both made this way, which is far harder than casting and leaves no seams. Numbers 10:2 uses the same technique for the silver trumpets.

Winged guardian figures, first stationed at Eden's gate in Genesis 3:24 and worked into the veil, the curtains, and the mercy seat here. Ezekiel 1 and 10 describe them in detail. They are not the plump infants of later European art.

A small altar, one cubit square and two high, roughly 18 inches by 18 by 36, made of acacia sheathed in gold with horns worked from the same piece and rings for carrying poles (37:25-28). It stood inside the Holy Place in front of the veil, not out in the courtyard where the animals were killed, and nothing but incense was burned on it (30:9). Luke 1:8-11 puts Zechariah at this altar when the angel appears to him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּצַלְאֵל (Betsalel), 'in the shadow of God'

stories.keyTakeaway: Bezalel and his workers construct the ark of the covenant with its atonement cover, the table for bread, the gold lampstand, and the altar of incense - all made of acacia wood overlaid with pure gold and fitted with carrying poles.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 38
summaryBullets: Bezalel constructed the altar of burnt offering from acacia wood. It was square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high. (38:1).

He made a grate of bronze mesh for the altar under its ledge, halfway up from the bottom. (38:4).
At the four corners of the bronze grate he cast four rings as holders for the poles. (38:5).
And he made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with bronze. (38:6).
Then he inserted the poles into the rings on the sides of the altar for carrying it. He made the altar with boards so that it was hollow. (38:7).
Next he made the bronze basin and its stand from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (38:8).
Then he constructed the courtyard. The south side of the courtyard was a hundred cubits long and had curtains of finely spun linen, (38:9).
with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and with silver hooks and bands on the posts. (38:10).
The north side was also a hundred cubits long, with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases. The hooks and bands of the posts were silver. (38:11).
The west side was fifty cubits long and had curtains, with ten posts and ten bases. The hooks and bands of the posts were silver. (38:12).
And the east side, toward the sunrise, was also fifty cubits long. (38:13).
The curtains on one side of the entrance were fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases. (38:14).
And the curtains on the other side were also fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases as well. (38:15).
All the curtains around the courtyard were made of finely spun linen. (38:16).
The bases for the posts were bronze, the hooks and bands were silver, and the plating for the tops of the posts was silver. So all the posts of the courtyard were banded with silver. (38:17).

The curtain for the entrance to the courtyard was embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. It was twenty cubits long and, like the curtains of the courtyard, five cubits high, (38:18).
with four posts and four bronze bases. Their hooks were silver, as well as the bands and the plating of their tops. (38:19).
All the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the surrounding courtyard were bronze. (38:20).

Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made everything that the LORD had commanded Moses. (38:22).
With him was Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver, designer, and embroiderer in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen. (38:23).
All the gold from the wave offering used for the work on the sanctuary totaled 29 talents and 730 shekels, according to the sanctuary shekel. (38:24).
The silver from those numbered among the congregation totaled 100 talents and 1,775 shekels, according to the sanctuary shekel— (38:25).
a beka per person, that is, half a shekel, according to the sanctuary shekel, from everyone twenty years of age or older who had crossed over to be numbered, a total of 603,550 men. (38:26).
The hundred talents of silver were used to cast the bases of the sanctuary and the bases of the veil— 100 bases from the 100 talents, one talent per base. (38:27).
With the 1,775 shekels [of silver] he made the hooks for the posts, overlaid their tops, and supplied bands for them. (38:28).
The bronze from the wave offering totaled 70 talents and 2,400 shekels. (38:29).
He used it to make the bases for the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the bronze altar and its bronze grating, all the utensils for the altar, (38:30).
the bases for the surrounding courtyard and its gate, and all the tent pegs for the tabernacle and its surrounding courtyard. (38:31).

Exodus 30:11-16: The half-shekel census ransom whose silver is accounted for in this inventory.
Numbers 1:45-46: The census total of 603,550 fighting men, the same count behind this weight of silver.
1 Samuel 2:22: Women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting appear again in Eli's day.
1 Corinthians 13:12: For now we see only a reflection as in a mirror, the polished bronze kind used here.

translationNotes.note: About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.
Half a shekel, about 0.2 oz (5.5 g). Used as the per-head temple-tax assessment in Exodus 38:26.

Both a weight (about 0.4 oz / 11 g) and a currency unit. In Old Testament economy a common laborer earned roughly half a shekel per month, so the 20 shekels paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28) was about three years of wages. The temple tax was half a shekel (Exodus 30:13); in New Testament reckoning that equaled two denarii / two days' wages.

At 3,000 shekels of about 11.4 grams to the talent, the inventory of Exodus 38:24-29 comes to roughly 1,000 kilograms of gold, 3,440 of silver, and 2,420 of bronze. In pounds that is roughly 2,200 of gold, 7,580 of silver, and 5,340 of bronze, all of it given voluntarily.

Exodus 38:27 spends the whole hundred talents of silver on a hundred sockets, one talent each. At about 34 kilograms apiece these are heavy cast blocks, and their weight is what held the upright frames steady in sand. The tabernacle stood on the census silver of every man counted.

Bronze discs polished to a shine; glass mirrors did not exist. The Hebrew tsovot is the same root as the word for an army serving in ranks, so these were women in organized service at the tent entrance, and 1 Samuel 2:22 mentions them again in Eli's day.

stories.keyTakeaway: The craftsmen build the bronze altar for burnt offerings and construct the courtyard around the tabernacle with its curtains, posts, and bases; Bezalel and Oholiab direct the work, and the total materials used - 29 talents of gold, 100 talents of silver, and 70 talents of bronze - are recorded.

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 39

Bezalel made the ephod of finely spun linen embroidered with gold, and with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn. (39:2).
They hammered out thin sheets of gold and cut threads from them to interweave with the blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen — the work of a skilled craftsman. (39:3).
They made shoulder pieces for the ephod, which were attached at two of its corners, so it could be fastened. (39:4).

And the skillfully woven waistband of the ephod was of one piece with the ephod, of the same workmanship — with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (39:5).
They mounted the onyx stones in gold filigree settings, engraved like a seal with the names of the sons of Israel. (39:6).
Then they fastened them on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel, as the LORD had commanded Moses. (39:7).
He made the breastpiece with the same workmanship as the ephod, with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen. (39:8).
It was square when folded over double, a span long and a span wide. (39:9).
And they mounted on it four rows of gemstones: The first row had a ruby, a topaz, and an emerald; (39:10).
the second row had a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond; (39:11).
the third row had a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst; (39:12).
and the fourth row had a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. These stones were mounted in gold filigree settings. (39:13).
The twelve stones corresponded to the names of the sons of Israel. Each stone was engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes. (39:14).
For the breastpiece they made braided chains like cords of pure gold. (39:15).
They also made two gold filigree settings and two gold rings, and fastened the two rings to the two corners of the breastpiece. (39:16).
Then they fastened the two gold chains to the two gold rings at the corners of the breastpiece, (39:17).
and they fastened the other ends of the two chains to the two filigree settings, attaching them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front. (39:18).

They made two additional gold rings and attached them to the bottom of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, on its front, near the seam just above its woven waistband. (39:20).

Then they tied the rings of the breastpiece to the rings of the ephod with a cord of blue yarn, so that the breastpiece was above the waistband of the ephod and would not swing out from the ephod, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (39:21).
They made the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth, the work of a weaver, (39:22).
with an opening in the center of the robe like that of a garment, with a collar around the opening so that it would not tear. (39:23).
They made pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen on the lower hem of the robe. (39:24).
They also made bells of pure gold and attached them around the hem between the pomegranates, (39:25).
alternating the bells and pomegranates around the lower hem of the robe to be worn for ministry, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (39:26).
For Aaron and his sons they made tunics of fine linen, the work of a weaver, (39:27).
as well as the turban of fine linen, the ornate headbands and undergarments of finely spun linen, (39:28).
and the sash of finely spun linen, embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (39:29).
They also made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and they engraved on it, like an inscription on a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD. (39:30).
Then they fastened to it a blue cord to mount it on the turban, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (39:31).
So all the work for the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting, was completed. The Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (39:32).
Then they brought the tabernacle to Moses: the tent with all its furnishings, its clasps, its frames, its crossbars, and its posts and bases; (39:33).
the covering of ram skins dyed red, the covering of fine leather, and the veil of the covering; (39:34).
the ark of the Testimony with its poles and the mercy seat; (39:35).
the table with all its utensils and the Bread of the Presence; (39:36).
the pure gold lampstand with its row of lamps and all its utensils, as well as the oil for the light; (39:37).
the gold altar, the anointing oil, the fragrant incense, and the curtain for the entrance to the tent; (39:38).
the bronze altar with its bronze grating, its poles, and all its utensils; the basin with its stand; (39:39).

the curtains of the courtyard with its posts and bases; the curtain for the gate of the courtyard, its ropes and tent pegs, and all the equipment for the service of the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting; (39:40).
and the woven garments for ministering in the sanctuary, both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests. (39:41).

Zechariah 3:3-5: Filthy garments are taken off Joshua the high priest and a clean turban set on his head.

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פַּחֵי הַזָּהָב (pachei ha-zahav), 'sheets of gold'

Gold can be beaten to a leaf a fraction of the thickness of paper, so a small weight of it goes a very long way. This is the only description of the technique in Scripture.

translationNotes.term: just as the LORD commanded Moses
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת־מֹשֶׁה (kaasher tsivvah YHWH et-Mosheh)

stories.title: ⛺ Exodus 40

Put the ark of the Testimony in it and screen off the ark with the veil. (40:3).
Then bring in the table and set out its arrangement; bring in the lampstand as well, and set up its lamps. (40:4).
Place the gold altar of incense in front of the ark of the Testimony, and hang the curtain at the entrance to the tabernacle. (40:5).
Place the altar of burnt offering in front of the entrance to the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting. (40:6).
And place the basin between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and put water in it. (40:7).
Set up the surrounding courtyard and hang the curtain for the entrance to the courtyard. (40:8).
Take the anointing oil and anoint the tabernacle and everything in it; consecrate it along with all its furnishings, and it shall be holy. (40:9).
Anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils; consecrate the altar, and it shall be most holy. (40:10).
Anoint the basin and its stand and consecrate them. (40:11).
Then bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water. (40:12).
And you are to clothe Aaron with the holy garments, anoint him, and consecrate him, so that he may serve Me as a priest. (40:13).
Bring his sons forward and clothe them with tunics. (40:14).
Anoint them just as you anointed their father, so that they may also serve Me as priests. Their anointing will qualify them for a permanent priesthood throughout their generations.” (40:15).
Moses did everything just as the LORD had commanded him. (40:16).
So the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year. (40:17).

Then he spread the tent over the tabernacle and put the covering over the tent, just as the LORD had commanded him. (40:19).
Moses took the Testimony and placed it in the ark, attaching the poles to the ark; and he set the mercy seat atop the ark. (40:20).
Then he brought the ark into the tabernacle, put up the veil for the screen, and shielded off the ark of the Testimony, just as the LORD had commanded him. (40:21).
Moses placed the table in the Tent of Meeting on the north side of the tabernacle, outside the veil. (40:22).
He arranged the bread on it before the LORD, just as the LORD had commanded him. (40:23).
He also placed the lampstand in the Tent of Meeting opposite the table on the south side of the tabernacle (40:24).
and set up the lamps before the LORD, just as the LORD had commanded him. (40:25).
Moses placed the gold altar in the Tent of Meeting, in front of the veil, (40:26).
and he burned fragrant incense on it, just as the LORD had commanded him. (40:27).
Then he put up the curtain at the entrance to the tabernacle. (40:28).

He placed the altar of burnt offering near the entrance to the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting, and offered on it the burnt offering and the grain offering, just as the LORD had commanded him. (40:29).
He placed the basin between the Tent of Meeting and the altar and put water in it for washing; (40:30).
and from it Moses, Aaron, and his sons washed their hands and feet. (40:31).

And Moses set up the courtyard around the tabernacle and the altar, and he hung the curtain for the entrance to the courtyard. So Moses finished the work. (40:33).
Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. (40:34).
Moses was unable to enter the Tent of Meeting because the cloud had settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. (40:35).

Numbers 9:15-23: The cloud over the tabernacle governs every stage of the march, by day and by night.
1 Kings 8:10-11: The cloud fills the house so that the priests cannot stand to minister.
2 Chronicles 5:13-14: The glory of the LORD fills the house of God at the temple's dedication.
Ezekiel 43:4-5: The glory of the LORD enters the house by the east gate and fills it.

Numbers 9:15-23 spells the rule out and says some stops lasted a day and some a year. Verse 40:38 adds that fire was in it by night, in the sight of the whole house of Israel.

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

translationNotes.term: the first day of the first month
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּשָׁנָה הַשֵּׁנִית (bachodesh harishon bashanah hashenit)
translationNotes.note: New Year's Day of the second year, in the month of Abib. intro:
Exodus (Hebrew: Shemot, "Names") was written by Moses during Israel's forty-year wilderness period between the departure from Egypt (c. 1446 BC) and Moses' death (c. 1406 BC). Moses composed the book in real time as he led the Israelite nation out of Egyptian slavery and through the early stages of the wilderness wandering. The Hebrew people had lived in Egypt for roughly 430 years since the time of the patriarch Joseph, growing from a single family of seventy into a population that the Egyptian Pharaohs forced into slave labor out of fear of their numbers. The historical setting is Egypt's 18th Dynasty (the New Kingdom), the height of Egyptian imperial power across the ancient Near East. The Pharaoh during Israel's deliverance is traditionally identified with Amenhotep II (reigning c. 1450-1425 BC), in the early Late Bronze Age. Jesus and the apostles attribute the Pentateuch, including Exodus, to Moses (Mark 12:26, Luke 24:44, John 5:46, Romans 10:5).

Exodus is the second book of the Pentateuch (the five books of Moses). Its Hebrew name Shemot comes from the opening words of the book, following the ancient Jewish convention of titling books by their opening line; the English title "Exodus" comes from the Greek Septuagint translation Exodos (3rd century BC), meaning "departure" or "going out." Hebrew manuscript fragments of Exodus were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 2nd and 1st centuries BC.
